Here's the full answer. ## Where the rows come from The "Fetch Overdue Payments" button on a Dunning draft (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/dunning/dunning.js:61-79`) calls `erpnext.utils.map_current_doc` against **`create_dunning`** in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/sales_invoice/mapper.py:569-618`, filtering invoices to `docstatus: 1, status: "Overdue"` and letting the user pick `Payment Schedule` child rows (rows can't be added manually — `cannot_add_rows`, dunning.js:40). `create_dunning` runs `get_mapped_doc` with two table maps: - **Sales Invoice → Dunning** (`field_map: {"customer_address": "customer_address", "parent": "sales_invoice"}`) — also copies `currency`/`customer`/`company` by same-name mapping. - **Payment Schedule → Overdue Payment** (`field_map: {"name": "payment_schedule", "parent": "sales_invoice"}`, `condition: doc.outstanding > 0 and getdate(doc.due_date) < getdate()`) — only installments that are both unpaid and past due. Because both child doctypes share fieldnames, Frappe's default mapping copies `outstanding`, `due_date`, `payment_term`, `invoice_portion` etc. straight across. ## How `row.outstanding` is computed — the `postprocess_dunning` fixup In `postprocess_dunning` (mapper.py:585-599), after the default mapping, when the source invoice has exactly **one** payment-schedule row, each matching `Overdue Payment` row is overridden: ```python if source.party_account_currency and source.party_account_currency != source.currency: row.outstanding = source.payment_schedule[0].outstanding # transaction currency else: row.outstanding = source.get("outstanding_amount") # account currency == invoice currency ``` The reason for the split is that the two candidate sources live in **different currencies**: - `Sales Invoice.outstanding_amount` is an *account-currency* figure. It is written by **`update_voucher_outstanding`** (`erpnext/accounts/utils.py:2175-2223`), which sets `outstanding_amount = flt(outstanding["outstanding_in_account_currency"])` from `QueryPaymentLedger.get_voucher_outstandings` — i.e., the residual against the **receivable (party) account's currency**, not the invoice's transaction currency. - `Payment Schedule.outstanding` is always in the invoice's **transaction currency**. It's seeded in `PaymentScheduleService.set_payment_schedule` (`erpnext/accounts/services/payment_schedule.py:94-108`) as `d.outstanding = d.payment_amount`, where `payment_amount` derives from `grand_total`, and kept in sync by **`PaymentEntry.update_payment_schedule`** (`payment_entry.py:805-897`), which converts each allocation back to transaction currency via **`get_allocated_amount_in_transaction_currency`** (payment_entry.py:898+) — using the *invoice's* own `conversion_rate`, so the schedule stays correct even when the paying Payment Entry posts at a different exchange rate. So when `party_account_currency == currency`, both figures coincide and the authoritative `outstanding_amount` is used; when they differ, copying `outstanding_amount` would put an account-currency number into a transaction-currency field, so the schedule's `outstanding` is used instead. ## Why that's correct for the mixed-currency case (#56006) Every downstream consumer of `Overdue Payment.outstanding` assumes transaction currency: - **`Dunning.validate_same_currency`** (dunning.py:79-97) throws unless each invoice's `currency` equals the Dunning's `currency` — the Dunning is denominated in the invoice currency. - **`Dunning.validate_overdue_payments`** (dunning.py:99-104): `overdue_days = posting_date − due_date` and `interest = outstanding × (rate_of_interest/100/365) × overdue_days` — computed directly on `row.outstanding`. - **`Dunning.validate_totals`** (dunning.py:106-111): `total_outstanding = Σ row.outstanding`, `total_interest = Σ row.interest`, `dunning_amount = total_interest + dunning_fee`, `base_dunning_amount = dunning_amount × conversion_rate`, `grand_total = total_outstanding + dunning_amount` — only coherent if `outstanding` is in the invoice currency (the JS handlers `calculate_interest`/`calculate_totals` in dunning.js mirror this, and `validate()` is re-run server-side in the postprocess anyway). Without the fixup, a USD invoice posting to an INR "Debtors" account would yield a Dunning row of 5000 labelled USD (with interest, `total_outstanding` and `grand_total` all inflated 50×). The regression test **`TestDunning.test_dunning_outstanding_uses_transaction_currency`** (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/dunning/test_dunning.py:156-185`) exercises exactly this, with `allow_multi_currency_invoices_against_single_party_account = 1`: a USD invoice at `conversion_rate=50`, `rate=100` against `Debtors - _TC` asserts `si.outstanding_amount == 5000.0` (INR), `si.payment_schedule[0].outstanding == 100.0` (USD), and finally `dunning.overdue_payments[0].outstanding == 100.0`. Two related notes: - **Multi-installment invoices** don't need the fixup: each Overdue Payment row is mapped per Payment Schedule row (already transaction currency), and the override only fires when `len(source.payment_schedule) == 1`. See `test_dunning_and_payment_against_partially_due_invoice` (test_dunning.py:88-124). - Downstream, **`update_linked_dunnings`** (dunning.py:207-266, hooked from `update_voucher_outstanding` at utils.py:2221) uses both the invoice `outstanding_amount` and each `Payment Schedule.outstanding` to flip linked Dunning status between Resolved/Unresolved as payments or credit notes settle the invoice.

I have the complete picture now. Here's the full answer. ## Where the rows come from `create_dunning(source_name, target_doc, ignore_permissions)` in **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/sales_invoice/mapper.py`** (lines 569–618) builds the Dunning with `get_mapped_doc`: - **Sales Invoice → Dunning**: same-named fields are copied (customer, company, `currency`, `conversion_rate`, …) plus `parent → sales_invoice`. - **Payment Schedule → Overdue Payment**: `name → payment_schedule`, `parent → sales_invoice`, and a row filter `doc.outstanding > 0 and getdate(doc.due_date) < getdate()` — only unpaid *and* past-due schedule rows become rows. Because the mapper copies same-named fields, each `OverduePayment.outstanding` initially inherits the `Payment Schedule.outstanding` value, and `OverduePayment` (erpnext/accounts/doctype/overdue_payment/overdue_payment.py) is a plain child doctype — it has no logic of its own; everything happens in the mapper and in `Dunning.validate()`. ## How the outstanding on each row is computed In `postprocess_dunning` (mapper.py lines 585–597), after the default `Dunning Type` (rate_of_interest, dunning_fee, income_account, etc.) is applied, the outstanding is set per row: ```python if source.payment_schedule and len(source.payment_schedule) == 1: for row in target.overdue_payments: if row.payment_schedule == source.payment_schedule[0].name: if source.party_account_currency and source.party_account_currency != source.currency: row.outstanding = source.payment_schedule[0].outstanding # transaction currency else: row.outstanding = source.get("outstanding_amount") # invoice-level value ``` - **Multi-schedule invoices** (payment terms with several instalments): the mapper's default field copy already carries each row's `outstanding` from its own `Payment Schedule` row, so nothing further is needed — the invoice-level `outstanding_amount` couldn't be split across rows anyway. - **Single-schedule invoices with matching currencies**: the fresher invoice-level `outstanding_amount` is used (it also reflects allocations that don't touch the schedule, e.g. some credit-note flows). - **Single-schedule invoice in a foreign currency against a differently-denominated receivable**: the payment schedule's own `outstanding` is used — and this is the #56006 fix. Then `target.validate()` runs `Dunning.validate()` (erpnext/accounts/doctype/dunning/dunning.py): - `validate_same_currency` — throws if any row's invoice currency ≠ the Dunning currency (this is why `OverduePayment.outstanding` can safely be denominated in the invoice/transaction currency). - `validate_overdue_payments` — `overdue_days = posting_date − due_date`, `interest = outstanding × rate_of_interest/100/365 × overdue_days` (computed on the transaction-currency outstanding). - `validate_totals` — `total_outstanding`, `total_interest`, `dunning_amount = total_interest + dunning_fee`, `base_dunning_amount = dunning_amount × conversion_rate`, `grand_total`. The client-side `dunning.js` (`calculate_totals`, interest calc) mirrors this with the same `row.outstanding`. ## Why the foreign-currency / different-receivable-currency case needs the branch There are two different "outstanding" values living on the invoice, denominated in different currencies: 1. **`Sales Invoice.outstanding_amount` — in the party account currency.** `update_outstanding_amt()` in **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/gl_entry/gl_entry.py`** (line 351) recomputes it from the GL ledger as `Σ debit_in_account_currency − Σ credit_in_account_currency` on the **receivable account** (`debit_to`), then writes it to `outstanding_amount`. So a USD invoice (rate 50, $100) posted against INR `Debtors - _TC` shows `outstanding_amount = 5000.0` INR, not 100 USD. 2. **`Payment Schedule.outstanding` — in the invoice's transaction currency.** It's initialized at invoice validation by `PaymentScheduleService.set_payment_schedule()` in **`erpnext/accounts/services/payment_schedule.py`** (`d.outstanding = d.payment_amount`, where `payment_amount` derives from `grand_total`, i.e. USD 100), and it is kept in transaction currency as payments allocate: `PaymentEntry.update_payment_schedule()` in **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py`** (line 805) does `ps.outstanding − allocated_amount` (and reverses on cancel), where `get_allocated_amount_in_transaction_currency()` (line 898) explicitly converts the payment entry's allocated amount back into the reference invoice's transaction currency — its docstring states: *"Payment Entry could be in base currency while reference's payment schedule is always in transaction currency."* Because `OverduePayment.outstanding` is displayed and used as an amount **in the invoice's transaction currency** (the Dunning's `validate_same_currency` guarantees the Dunning is in that currency, and interest/`total_outstanding`/`grand_total` are all derived from it), copying the 5000 INR value into it would mislabel it as 5000 USD — inflating the outstanding, the interest, and the grand total by the conversion rate. The branch on `party_account_currency != currency` prevents exactly that by pulling the schedule's transaction-currency outstanding instead. (The `$56006` comment in the mapper documents this.) ## Proof it behaves correctly The regression test **`test_dunning_outstanding_uses_transaction_currency`** in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/dunning/test_dunning.py` (lines 155–185) covers precisely this scenario (with `allow_multi_currency_invoices_against_single_party_account` enabled): - USD invoice, rate 100, `conversion_rate=50`, `debit_to="Debtors - _TC"` (INR receivable) - Asserts `si.outstanding_amount == 5000.0` (INR, party account currency) and `si.payment_schedule[0].outstanding == 100.0` (USD) - After `create_dunning_from_sales_invoice(...)`, asserts `dunning.overdue_payments[0].outstanding == 100.0` — *"Must reflect 100 USD, not 5000 INR mislabelled as USD."* **Summary**: the outstanding on each Overdue Payment row comes from the invoice's Payment Schedule rows (filtered to unpaid + overdue ones); for single-schedule invoices the mapper explicitly chooses `payment_schedule[0].outstanding` (transaction currency) whenever the invoice currency differs from the receivable account's currency, falling back to the invoice-level `outstanding_amount` (party account currency) only when the two currencies coincide — so interest, totals and the dunning letter are always computed in the currency the customer is actually being dunned in.

Because a whitelisted (`@frappe.whitelist()`) method is callable by **any** authenticated user over HTTP regardless of what the form shows, each one re-checks permissions server-side before touching data: ## 1. Attribute autocomplete — `get_item_attribute` - **Client:** `item.js:1483` → `erpnext.stock.doctype.item.item.get_item_attribute` - **Server:** `item.py:1525-1535` - **Guard:** the first thing it does is ```python if not frappe.has_permission("Item"): frappe.throw(_("No Permission")) ``` `frappe.has_permission("Item")` with no `ptype` defaults to **read** permission on the Item doctype (checking the user's role permissions and user-level "User Permission" restrictions). Only then does it run the `frappe.get_all("Item Attribute Value", ...)` LIKE query for the autocomplete suggestions. So a user who cannot even read Items gets a "No Permission" thrown exception instead of attribute data. ## 2. Item price preview — `get_item_prices` - **Client:** `item.js:861` → `erpnext.stock.doctype.item.item.get_item_prices` - **Server:** `item.py:1588-1623` - **Guard:** ```python if not frappe.has_permission("Item Price", "read"): frappe.throw(_("Not permitted"), frappe.PermissionError) ``` This is deliberately **not** an Item check — the endpoint returns Item Price rows, so it requires explicit **read permission on the Item Price doctype** (and again, role/user-permission checks apply). If allowed, it runs the pypika query against `Item Price` (non-cancelled, valid-dated rows, limit 11 → first 10 + `has_more`). A user with Item read access but no Item Price role gets `frappe.PermissionError`. The client call at `item.js:861` is only made from the Item Prices tab logic, but the server check is what actually protects the data. ## 3. Opening stock creation — `make_opening_stock_entry` - **Client:** `item.js:1001` → `erpnext.stock.doctype.item.item.make_opening_stock_entry` - **Server:** `item.py:1626-1696` - **Guard:** this is a **write** operation (it inserts and submits a `Stock Reconciliation` via `create_opening_stock_reconciliation`, `item.py:1699-1728`), so the check is: ```python if not frappe.has_permission("Item", "write", item_code): frappe.throw(_("Not permitted"), frappe.PermissionError) ``` Note it passes `item_code` as the third argument, so `frappe.has_permission` also enforces **user permissions** (the "User Permissions" / `frappe.user.get_perms` restrictions limiting which specific Item documents the user may act on), not just the doctype-level write role. After the permission gate, additional business validation runs (stock item only, no serial/batch items — those must go through Stock Reconciliation form, no prior stock ledger entries, qty > 0, non-negative valuation rate, warehouse belongs to the company), and it then creates and submits the opening `Stock Reconciliation` and posts a comment/alert. ## Summary | Endpoint | File / lines | Permission check | |---|---|---| | `get_item_attribute` | `item.py:1525-1535` | `frappe.has_permission("Item")` (read on Item) | | `get_item_prices` | `item.py:1588-1592` | `frappe.has_permission("Item Price", "read")` (read on Item Price) | | `make_opening_stock_entry` | `item.py:1634-1635` | `frappe.has_permission("Item", "write", item_code)` (write on that specific Item doc, incl. user permissions) | In every case the pattern is the same defensive idiom for whitelisted endpoints: the check is the **first statement** in the function, raises via `frappe.throw` (with `frappe.PermissionError` for the latter two, so the client gets a 403-style error), and nothing is read from or written to the database until the check passes.

The JS callers are in `erpnext/stock/doctype/item/item.js` (`get_item_attribute` at line 1483, `get_item_prices` at line 861, `make_opening_stock_entry` at line 1001). ## 1. Attribute autocomplete — `get_item_attribute(item.py:1525–1535)` ```python @frappe.whitelist() def get_item_attribute(parent: str, attribute_value: str = ""): """Used for providing auto-completions in child table.""" if not frappe.has_permission("Item"): frappe.throw(_("No Permission")) return frappe.get_all("Item Attribute Value", ...) ``` - **Guard:** an explicit `frappe.has_permission("Item")` check (default `ptype="read"` — the user must have read access to the Item doctype) at the very top, throwing `"No Permission"`. - **Why it's needed:** the query uses `frappe.get_all("Item Attribute Value", ...)`, which by design **ignores ORM permission filtering** (`frappe.get_all` ≡ `get_list(..., ignore_permissions=True)`). Without the manual check, any user could enumerate every Item Attribute's values by passing arbitrary `parent` names. The check anchors authorization to Item read access instead of the child/parent doctype the client sends. ## 2. Item price previews — `get_item_prices(item.py:1588–1623)` ```python @frappe.whitelist() def get_item_prices(item_code: str): """Fetch valid item prices for the item prices tab.""" if not frappe.has_permission("Item Price", "read"): frappe.throw(_("Not permitted"), frappe.PermissionError) ... prices = (frappe.qb.from_(ItemPrice) ... .run(as_dict=True)) ``` - **Guard:** an explicit, permission-*type*-specific check — `frappe.has_permission("Item Price", "read")` — throwing a typed `frappe.PermissionError` (renders as HTTP 403). - **Why it's needed:** this is the strongest example of why whitelisted methods must self-check: the function runs a **raw `frappe.qb` query directly against the `Item Price` table** (`.run()` applies no permission filtering at all — not even what `frappe.get_list` would do). The explicit `has_permission` is the *only* line of defense preventing a user who can open the Item form (e.g., an Item-only role) from reading price list rates, customer/supplier-specific prices, currencies, etc., for any item code they type. ## 3. Opening stock creation — `make_opening_stock_entry(item.py:1626–1696)` ```python @frappe.whitelist() def make_opening_stock_entry(item_code, company, qty, valuation_rate, warehouse=None): if not frappe.has_permission("Item", "write", item_code): frappe.throw(_("Not permitted"), frappe.PermissionError) item = frappe.get_doc("Item", item_code) ... # business validations stock_reco = create_opening_stock_reconciliation(...) ``` This one has **two layers**: - **Layer 1 — explicit document-level check:** `frappe.has_permission("Item", "write", item_code)` — note it passes the *specific document name*, so besides role-based "write" on Item, Frappe's **User Permissions / doc-permission queries** for that exact Item are also enforced. Throws `frappe.PermissionError`. (Compare with #1 and #2, which are doctype-level read checks.) - **Layer 2 — framework checks on the resulting document:** the helper `create_opening_stock_reconciliation` (item.py:1699–1730) builds a `Stock Reconciliation` ("Opening Stock") and calls plain `stock_reco.insert()` and `stock_reco.submit()` — **without** `ignore_permissions`. `Document.insert()`/`submit()` therefore run Frappe's built-in `check_permission("create")` / `check_permission("submit")`, so a user must *also* have create/submit rights on Stock Reconciliation for the operation to actually complete. This is the same pattern as `make_stock_entry` in `stock_entry_utils.py` (also whitelisted, no explicit check, but guarded solely by `s.insert()`/`s.submit()`). Additional non-permission guards in the same function prevent misuse even by an authorized user: item must be `is_stock_item`, serial/batch items are rejected (must use the Stock Reconciliation form), `stock_ledger_created()` blocks re-opening, qty > 0, non-negative valuation rate, warehouse must belong to `company`, and a Temporary opening account must exist. ## Summary table | Endpoint (item.py) | Client trigger (item.js) | Guard | |---|---|---| | `get_item_attribute` :1525 | attribute autocomplete input :1483 | `frappe.has_permission("Item")` → generic "No Permission" throw (needed because `frappe.get_all` skips permissions) | | `get_item_prices` :1588 | prices tab load :860 | `frappe.has_permission("Item Price", "read")` → `frappe.PermissionError` (needed because raw `frappe.qb` query skips permissions) | | `make_opening_stock_entry` :1626 | "Add Opening Stock" dialog :1000 | `frappe.has_permission("Item", "write", item_code)` on the *specific doc* → `frappe.PermissionError`, **plus** implicit create/submit checks via `Stock Reconciliation.insert()/submit()` | The common theme: whenever a whitelisted method reads/writes data through a channel that bypasses Frappe's standard ORM permission enforcement (`frappe.get_all` or `frappe.qb ... .run()`), ERPNext adds an explicit `frappe.has_permission(...)` as the first statement; the write path additionally inherits the framework's insert/submit permission checks.

final answer
I've traced the full mechanism. Here's how ERPNext keeps "promised" stock out of reach of other shipments. ## 1. Where the promise is recorded The promise is a **Stock Reservation Entry (SRE)** — `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reservation_entry/stock_reservation_entry.py`. Each SRE pins a qty of an item in a specific warehouse to a specific voucher row (`voucher_type`/`voucher_no`/`voucher_detail_no`, e.g. a Sales Order Item), with `reserved_qty`, `delivered_qty`, `transferred_qty`, `consumed_qty`, a `status`, and — for serial/batch items — exact serials/batches in the `sb_entries` child table (`reservation_based_on = "Qty" | "Serial and Batch"`). Creation flow: - `SalesOrder.on_submit` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/sales_order.py:450-471`): if the **Reserve Stock** flag is set, calls `create_stock_reservation_entries()` → `SalesOrderStockReservation.create_stock_reservation_entries()` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/services/reservation.py`) → **`create_stock_reservation_entries_for_so_items()`** (`stock_reservation_entry.py:1606`), which skips non-stock items/group warehouses, computes `get_unreserved_qty()` (SO qty − delivered − already reserved), and creates an SRE for `min(unreserved_qty, available_qty_to_reserve)`. On SO cancel, `cancel_stock_reservation_entries()` reverses them. - A Pick List can reserve exactly what was picked: `PickList.create_stock_reservation_entries()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/pick_list/pick_list.py:498`), passing picked serial/batch bundles. - Independently, a soft rollup lives on **Bin**: `get_reserved_qty()` in `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py` sums undelivered qty of open Sales Orders into `Bin.reserved_qty` (via `update_bin_qty()`, called from `SalesOrder.update_reserved_qty` → `SalesOrderStockReservation.update_reserved_qty`), and SRE-based reserved stock is rolled into `Bin.reserved_stock` by `Bin.update_reserved_stock()` → `get_sre_reserved_qty_for_item_and_warehouse()` (`bin.py:217-226`). ## 2. How "still available to promise" is calculated - **`get_available_qty_to_reserve(item_code, warehouse, batch_no=None, ignore_sre=None)`** (`stock_reservation_entry.py:693`) = `get_stock_balance()` (`erpnext/stock/utils.py:99`, last SLE `qty_after_transaction`) **minus** `Sum(reserved_qty − delivered_qty − transferred_qty − consumed_qty)` over submitted SREs where `delivered_qty < reserved_qty`. Note it takes `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` locks on the SRE rows (and the Bin row on Postgres) so two concurrent reservations can't both claim the same units. - Per-SO ceiling: `StockReservationEntry.validate_with_allowed_qty()` (`stock_reservation_entry.py:574`) — allowed = **min(available-to-reserve, voucher_qty − delivered_qty − already-reserved-for-that-row)** via `get_sre_reserved_qty_for_voucher_detail_no()`; over-reserving throws with the whole formula spelled out. - Serial level: `get_available_serial_nos_to_reserve()` (`stock_reservation_entry.py:749`); batch level: the `batch_no` branch of `get_available_qty_to_reserve` → `get_batch_qty()`. - Planning/report level: **`Bin.projected_qty`** = `actual + ordered + indented + planned − reserved_qty − reserved_for_production − reserved_for_sub_contract − reserved_for_production_plan`, computed by `Bin.set_projected_qty()` (`bin.py:66-76`) and `update_qty()` (`bin.py:251`). This is the ATP number shown on Sales Order items (`SalesOrder.validate_for_items`, `sales_order.py:310`), production planning, and the stock dashboard (`erpnext/stock/dashboard/item_dashboard.py`, which also surfaces SRE-based `reserved_stock`). ## 3. How an unrelated shipment is stopped Three layers: **a) At reservation time** — a second customer's SO can't reserve the same units because `get_available_qty_to_reserve` subtracts existing SREs (with row locks); the user just gets "Stock not available to reserve…". **b) At stock-ledger time (the hard stop)** — `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`: - `make_sl_entries()` (line 104) loads `Bin.reserved_stock` into `args.reserved_stock` (line 161) for every stock posting. - During ledger processing, `update_entries_after.validate_negative_stock()` (line 1352) computes `diff = qty_after_transaction + actual_qty − reserved_stock` and raises `NegativeStockError` if negative — with the message at lines 1860-1868: *"As X units are reserved for other sales orders, you are allowed to consume only Y units."* So an unrelated Delivery Note can physically issue at most `balance − reserved`. - For backdated postings: `update_qty_in_future_sle()` (line 2212) → `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle()` (line 2355) → **`validate_reserved_stock()`** (line 2470), which throws ("Reserved Stock") if `get_stock_balance − reserved_stock < 0`. - Serial/batch granular stop: `SerialandBatchBundle.validate_serial_nos` → `get_serial_no_reservation()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py:313, 2818`) throws *"Serial No … is reserved for Sales Order … via Stock Reservation Entry"*; outward serial selection in `get_available_serial_nos()` (lines 2445-2467, via `get_reserved_serial_nos_for_sre` / `get_reserved_serial_nos_for_voucher` / `get_other_doc_reserved_serials`) only offers serials reserved for *that* voucher; batches are filtered by `get_reserved_batches_for_sre()` (line 2921). Stock Reconciliation has its own guard: `StockReconciliation.validate_reserved_stock` (`stock_reconciliation.py:829`). **c) At delivery-routing time** — a DN against a reserved SO must ship from the reserved warehouse: `DeliveryNote.validate_against_stock_reservation_entries()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/delivery_note/delivery_note.py:544`, called from `validate` at line 296) uses `get_sre_reserved_warehouses_for_voucher()` and throws **"Stock Reservation Warehouse Mismatch"** otherwise. Building the DN from "Create > Reserved Stock" uses `make_delivery_note(for_reserved_stock=True)` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/mapper.py:232`), which maps DN rows/serials straight from `get_sre_details_for_voucher()` / `get_ssb_bundle_for_voucher()`. **Finally, consuming the promise:** `DeliveryNote.on_submit` calls `SellingController.update_stock_reservation_entries()` (`erpnext/controllers/selling_controller.py:930`) *before* `update_stock_ledger()` (delivery_note.py:507-511, with a comment explaining the ordering): it walks the SO's SREs in creation order, increments `delivered_qty` (matching serial/batch rows for `"Serial and Batch"` reservations), updates the SRE `status`, and refreshes `Bin.reserved_stock` via `update_reserved_stock_in_bin()`. That decrement is what keeps the ledger's `balance − reserved ≥ 0` check green for the rightful shipment while still blocking everyone else. Cancelling a DN reverses this via `update_unreserved_qty_in_sre()` (`stock_reservation_entry.py:148`). Related Stock Settings toggles used throughout: `enable_stock_reservation`, `auto_reserve_stock`, `allow_partial_reservation`, `auto_reserve_serial_and_batch` (see `reservation.py:25-33` and `validate_stock_reservation_settings` at `stock_reservation_entry.py:675`).

final answer
I have the full picture now. Here's how ERPNext keeps promised stock out of reach of other shipments: ## 1. Where the promise is recorded — the `Stock Reservation Entry` (SRE) The promise lives in the **`Stock Reservation Entry`** doctype (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reservation_entry/stock_reservation_entry.py`). Each SRE links the stock to the promising document via `voucher_type` / `voucher_no` / `voucher_detail_no` (e.g. "Sales Order SO-0001, row abc"), plus `item_code`, `warehouse`, `reserved_qty`, and the consumption counters `delivered_qty`, `transferred_qty`, `consumed_qty`, with `reservation_based_on` = `Qty` or `Serial and Batch`. - Reservation must be enabled (`enable_stock_reservation` in Stock Settings), enforced by `validate_stock_reservation_settings` (line 675) — only Sales Order is an allowed voucher. - The promise is created at **Sales Order submit**: `SalesOrder.on_submit` → `SalesOrder.create_stock_reservation_entries` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/sales_order.py:658`) → `SalesOrderStockReservation.create_stock_reservation_entries` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/services/reservation.py`) → the module-level `create_stock_reservation_entries_for_so_items` (SRE file, line 1606), which reserves for SO items flagged `reserve_stock`. Pick Lists (`PickList.create_stock_reservation_entries`, `erpnext/stock/doctype/pick_list/pick_list.py:498`) and Purchase Receipts can add reservations against the same SO rows. - On submit, `StockReservationEntry.update_reserved_stock_in_bin` (line 523) → `Bin.update_reserved_stock` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/bin/bin.py:217`) → **`get_sre_reserved_qty_for_item_and_warehouse`** (line 803) writes the hard number onto the warehouse's **`Bin.reserved_stock`** = `Σ(reserved_qty − delivered_qty − transferred_qty − consumed_qty)` over submitted SREs. When the promised shipment actually happens, `SellingController.update_stock_reservation_entries` (`erpnext/controllers/selling_controller.py:930`, called from Delivery Note / Sales Invoice `on_submit`/`on_cancel`) increments `delivered_qty` on the matching SREs, progressively releasing the promise. ## 2. How "still available to promise" is calculated **`get_available_qty_to_reserve`** (SRE file, line 693) is the ATP function: ``` get_stock_balance(item_code, warehouse) # actual qty from Stock Ledger Entry − Σ(reserved_qty − delivered_qty − transferred_qty − consumed_qty) over submitted SREs where delivered_qty < reserved_qty ``` - `get_stock_balance` (`erpnext/stock/utils.py:99`) reads `qty_after_transaction` from the latest SLE. - For batched items it delegates to `get_batch_qty(..., ignore_voucher_nos=[sre])` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/batch/batch.py:235`); for serial items there's `get_available_serial_nos_to_reserve` (line 749). The query takes `FOR UPDATE` row locks on the SREs/Bin so two concurrent reservations can't both claim the same qty. - The class method `StockReservation.get_available_qty_to_reserve` (line 1270) is the same logic used when creating SREs for Work Orders/Production Plans; per-SO remaining promise is computed by `SalesOrderStockReservation.has_unreserved_stock` + `get_unreserved_qty` (reservation service, lines 60–75). - Separately, there's a **soft, informational** layer: `Bin.reserved_qty` (open SOs, maintained by `stock_balance.get_reserved_qty` via `SalesOrderStockReservation.update_reserved_qty`, line 35) feeds `Bin.set_projected_qty` (`bin.py:66`: `projected_qty = actual + ordered + indented + planned − reserved_…`) and is displayed via `get_bin_details` (`erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1544`). That layer only informs planners — it does **not** block anything. ## 3. How an unrelated shipment is stopped **Hard stop in the stock ledger.** Every stock posting gets `Bin.reserved_stock` injected into its validation args (`stock_ledger.py:161`, passed through `repost_current_voucher` at line 190). Then: - **`StockLedger.update_entries_after.validate_negative_stock`** (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1352`) computes `diff = qty_after_transaction + actual_qty − reserved_stock` — reserved stock is treated as a floor. An unlinked delivery that would eat into it raises `NegativeStockError`, and the error message at lines 1860–1868 explicitly says *"As N units are reserved for other sales orders, you are allowed to consume only M units"* / *"the full stock is reserved for other transactions, you're not allowed to consume the stock"*. - **`validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle`** (line 2355) → **`validate_reserved_stock`** (line 2470) re-checks `balance_qty − reserved_stock ≥ 0` during future-SLE reposting, throwing with title "Reserved Stock". - **Serial/batch granularity:** `validate_reserved_serial_nos` / `validate_reserved_batch_nos` (`stock_ledger.py:2487`, `2503`) throw if another voucher picks reserved serials/batches, and `SerialBatchBundleService.validate_reserved_batches` (`erpnext/stock/services/serial_batch_bundle_service.py:587`, invoked from `erpnext/stock/services/stock_ledger_service.py:217`) blocks reserved batches on Delivery Note / Sales Invoice / Stock Entry unless the voucher references the SO that owns the reservation. **Warehouse stop on the promised shipment itself.** `DeliveryNote.validate_against_stock_reservation_entries` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/delivery_note/delivery_note.py:544`) requires that a DN row referencing a reserved SO row deliver *from the reserved warehouse* (`get_sre_reserved_warehouses_for_voucher`, SRE line 881) or it throws "Stock Reservation Warehouse Mismatch" — and conversely, delivering against the SO consumes the SRE's `delivered_qty`, releasing the promise. In short: **the promise is the SRE** (SO row ↔ warehouse ↔ qty/serial/batch), it aggregates into `Bin.reserved_stock`, ATP is `get_available_qty_to_reserve` (actual balance minus outstanding reservations), and the guard is the stock-ledger negative-stock check that subtracts `reserved_stock` — so an unrelated shipment can drain a warehouse only down to the reserved level, never into it.

## How ERPNext keeps promised stock away from other customers ERPNext records the promise as a **Stock Reservation Entry (SRE)** and uses it at three levels: a per-customer record of the promise, a rollup that drives the "available to promise" numbers, and enforcement at delivery/picking time. ### 1. Where the promise is recorded — `Stock Reservation Entry` File: `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reservation_entry/stock_reservation_entry.py` (class `StockReservationEntry`, L17). Each SRE pins stock to a specific demand document via `voucher_type` / `voucher_no` / `voucher_detail_no` (e.g. *Sales Order* + the exact SO item row), plus `item_code`, `warehouse`, `reserved_qty`, and consumption counters `delivered_qty`, `transferred_qty`, `consumed_qty`. For serialized/batched items, `reservation_based_on = "Serial and Batch"` and the child table `sb_entries` (Serial and Batch Entry) pins the **exact serial nos / batches**. The promise is created when a Sales Order with **Reserve Stock** checked is submitted (gated by `Stock Settings.enable_stock_reservation`, checked in `validate_stock_reservation_settings`, L675): - `SalesOrder.on_submit` → `create_stock_reservation_entries()` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/sales_order.py` L470-471, 658) - → `SalesOrderStockReservation.create_stock_reservation_entries` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/services/reservation.py` L76) - → `create_stock_reservation_entries_for_so_items` / `StockReservation.make_stock_reservation_entries` (stock_reservation_entry.py L1606, L1164), which creates and submits one SRE per item row. On SO cancel the SREs are cancelled (`sales_order.py` L497 → `cancel_stock_reservation_entries`, stock_reservation_entry.py L1815). `auto_reserve_stock` in Stock Settings turns the flag on automatically (`enable_auto_reserve_stock`, reservation.py L31). ### 2. How "still available to promise" is calculated - **`get_available_qty_to_reserve(item_code, warehouse)`** (stock_reservation_entry.py L693): `get_stock_balance()` (erpnext/stock/utils.py) **minus** `Σ(reserved_qty − delivered_qty − transferred_qty − consumed_qty)` over submitted SREs where `delivered_qty < reserved_qty`. It takes `FOR UPDATE` locks (Bin row on postgres, SRE rows on MariaDB) so two concurrent reservations can't claim the same free units. The per-document variant is `StockReservation.get_available_qty_to_reserve` (L1270); `make_stock_reservation_entries` (L1200-1209) reserves `min(requested, available)` and warns "Stock not available to reserve" if nothing is free — so a **second customer's order cannot promise the same units**. Serialized items use `get_available_serial_nos_to_reserve` (L749), which subtracts serial nos already pinned by other SREs. - **Bin rollup**: `StockReservationEntry.update_reserved_stock_in_bin` (L523) → `Bin.update_reserved_stock` (erpnext/stock/doctype/bin/bin.py L217) → `get_sre_reserved_qty_for_item_and_warehouse` (L803) maintains `Bin.reserved_stock`. Independently, the classic aggregate from open Sales Order rows is computed by `get_reserved_qty` (erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py L89) and pushed to the Bin by `update_bin_qty` in `SalesOrderStockReservation.update_reserved_qty` (reservation.py L35, wired at sales_order.py L544-545). - **`Bin.set_projected_qty`** (bin.py L66): `projected_qty = actual + ordered + indented + planned − reserved − reserved_for_production − reserved_for_sub_contract − reserved_for_production_plan` — this is the "free to promise" figure surfaced by the Stock Projected Qty and Reserved Stock reports (`erpnext/stock/report/stock_projected_qty/`, `erpnext/stock/report/reserved_stock/`). SRE progress is also mirrored onto the source rows (`stock_reserved_qty` on Sales Order Item / Pick List Item) by `update_reserved_qty_in_voucher` (L459) and `update_reserved_qty_in_pick_list` (L497). ### 3. How it stops an unrelated shipment from taking that stock - **Right customer, smooth path**: `make_delivery_note` in `erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/mapper.py` (L232, `for_reserved_stock`) fetches the SO's SREs via `get_sre_details_for_voucher` / `get_ssb_bundle_for_voucher` (L347, 402-404) so the Delivery Note ships exactly the reserved serial nos/batches. On submit, `DeliveryNote.on_submit` → `update_stock_reservation_entries()` (delivery_note.py L507/524; same hook in sales_invoice.py L452/542, stock_entry.py L337/382) → `SellingController.update_stock_reservation_entries` (erpnext/controllers/selling_controller.py L930), which matches DN rows to the SRE by `voucher_no` + `so_detail` + warehouse (L968-982) and bumps `SRE.delivered_qty`, freeing the promise (`StockReservationEntry.update_status`, L530, marks Delivered/Partially Delivered). - **Wrong customer, serial/batch items — hard block**: any voucher building a Serial and Batch Bundle runs `validate_serial_nos_warehouse_and_batch` (erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py ~L280-326). If a serial no is held by an SRE, `get_serial_no_reservation` (L2819) finds it and the shipment is rejected with `SerialNoWarehouseError`: *"Serial No … is reserved for Sales Order … via [SRE]. Please use an unreserved serial number or cancel the reservation."* Auto-picking helpers (`get_available_serial_nos`, reserved-serial/batch queries at L2786/2922) never offer reserved serial nos to other vouchers. - **Promise survives stock movements**: `StockReservation.transfer_reservation_entries_to` (L1296) and `StockController.update_stock_reservation_entries` (erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py L402) track `transferred_qty`/`consumed_qty` (e.g. Send to Subcontractor), so moving reserved stock between internal vouchers doesn't silently release the promise. SRE edits after partial delivery are blocked by `can_be_updated` (L555) and over-reservation by `validate_with_allowed_qty` (L574). - **Qty-based plain stock**: there is no physical stock-ledger block (ledger only enforces negative-stock rules), but the reservation is protected economically — `get_available_qty_to_reserve` prevents double-promising, `Bin.projected_qty`/`reserved_stock` keep planners and Pick Lists from seeing that stock as free, and the pick list itself can create reservations against the SO (`erpnext/stock/doctype/pick_list/pick_list.py` `create_stock_reservation_entries`, L498 → `so_doc.create_stock_reservation_entries`), tying the pick to the same customer's promise.

final answer
Here's the complete mechanism, traced through the code. ## 1. Where the promise is recorded There are two layers — a soft promise on the `Bin`, and a hard, physical reservation: **Soft promise — `Bin.reserved_qty` (always on).** When a Sales Order is submitted, `SalesOrder.on_submit` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/sales_order.py:450`) calls `SalesOrder.update_reserved_qty()` → `SalesOrderStockReservation.update_reserved_qty` (`erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/services/reservation.py:35`). That collects every (item, warehouse) pair from SO rows (or `Packed Items` for product bundles) and calls: - `get_reserved_qty(item_code, warehouse)` — `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:89`. Sums `(stock_qty − delivered_qty)` over submitted, non‑Closed/On‑Hold Sales Orders (`net_reserved / so_item.qty` prorates partial deliveries; `dont_reserve_sales_order_qty_on_sales_return` in Selling Settings subtracts `returned_qty`). Items marked `delivered_by_supplier` are excluded. - `update_bin_qty(item_code, warehouse, {"reserved_qty": ...})` — `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:274`, which writes the rollup onto the `Bin` and re-derives `projected_qty` via `Bin.set_projected_qty()`. **Hard promise — the `Stock Reservation Entry` (SRE) doctype.** If Stock Settings → *Enable Stock Reservation* is on and the order/row has `reserve_stock` (auto-set by `SalesOrderStockReservation.enable_auto_reserve_stock` from `auto_reserve_stock`), `SalesOrder.on_submit` also calls `create_stock_reservation_entries()` (`sales_order.py:470-471`) → `SalesOrderStockReservation.create_stock_reservation_entries` → `create_stock_reservation_entries_for_so_items` and the `StockReservation` engine in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reservation_entry/stock_reservation_entry.py`. Each SRE pins a qty: `voucher_type="Sales Order"`, `voucher_no`, `voucher_detail_no` (the SO row), `item_code`, `warehouse`, `reserved_qty`, `available_qty`, and for serialized/batched items specific `sb_entries` (`reservation_based_on = "Serial and Batch"`). The SRE is literally the "this stock belongs to this customer's order" record. Purchase Receipts can pre-reserve incoming goods for an SO the same way (`PurchaseReceiptStockReservation.reserve_stock_for_sales_order`, `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/reservation.py:21`, gated by `auto_reserve_stock_for_sales_order_on_purchase`). On SRE submit, `StockReservationEntry.on_submit` → `update_reserved_stock_in_bin` (stock_reservation_entry.py:523) → `Bin.update_reserved_stock` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/bin/bin.py:217`) → `get_sre_reserved_qty_for_item_and_warehouse` (stock_reservation_entry.py:803) = `Sum(reserved_qty − delivered_qty − transferred_qty − consumed_qty)` over submitted SREs, stored as **`Bin.reserved_stock`** — the physically cordoned-off qty. ## 2. How "still available to promise" is calculated `Bin.set_projected_qty` — `erpnext/stock/doctype/bin/bin.py:66`: ```python projected_qty = actual_qty + ordered_qty + indented_qty + planned_qty − reserved_qty − reserved_qty_for_production − reserved_qty_for_sub_contract − reserved_qty_for_production_plan ``` i.e. on-hand + incoming − everything already promised (SOs, work orders, subcontracting, production plans). The UI reads it via `get_projected_qty(item_code, warehouse)` (`erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1535`) and `get_bin_details` (`bin.py:233`). Each `reserved_qty_*` component is recomputed from its source documents (`get_reserved_qty`, `get_indented_qty`, `get_ordered_qty`, `get_planned_qty` in stock_balance.py; `get_reserved_qty_for_production_plan` in `erpnext/manufacturing/doctype/production_plan/services/reservation.py:30`); `Bin.recalculate_qty` (bin.py:40) recomputes all of them at once. Separately, the *physically free* stock is `actual_qty − Bin.reserved_stock` (SRE-based). ## 3. How it stops an unrelated shipment from taking the stock **Ledger-level guard (the hard block).** Every outgoing Stock Ledger Entry goes through `make_sl_entries` (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:104`) into the repost engine `update_entries_after` (`stock_ledger.py:587`), whose `__init__` loads `self.reserved_stock = self.get_reserved_stock()` (`stock_ledger.py:631` — `Sum(reserved_qty − delivered_qty − transferred_qty − consumed_qty)` for docstatus-1 SREs of that item+warehouse). Then `validate_negative_stock(sle)` (`stock_ledger.py:1352`) enforces: ```python diff = qty_after_transaction + actual_qty − reserved_stock ``` If that goes negative → `NegativeStockError`. So a Delivery Note for a *different* customer, a stock write-off, or a Stock Reconciliation that would eat into reserved units is rejected with "Insufficient Stock" — the reserved qty is invisible to them. (The test suite even covers this: `test_reserved_stock_cannot_be_delivered_against_a_different_sales_order`.) Crucially, `StockSettings.validate_stock_reservation` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_settings/stock_settings.py:209`) forbids enabling "Allow Negative Stock" while Stock Reservation is on, so this guard can't be bypassed. **Backdated postings** are also covered: `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle` (`stock_ledger.py:2355`) calls `validate_reserved_stock(args)` (`stock_ledger.py:2470`), throwing if `get_stock_balance(item, warehouse) − reserved_stock < 0`, with the message "… needed in … to complete this transaction." **Serial/batch-level guard.** `validate_reserved_serial_nos` / `validate_reserved_batch_nos` (`stock_ledger.py:2487/2503`) block using serial nos or batches pinned in an SRE ("Serial Nos are reserved in Stock Reservation Entries…"), and auto-picking (`get_auto_batch_nos` / `get_auto_serial_nos` in stock_reservation_entry.py) filters reserved ones out of the candidate list. Stock Reconciliation has its own guard, `StockReconciliation.validate_reserved_stock` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reconciliation/stock_reconciliation.py:829`), so a count can't wipe out reserved stock either. **The rightful order's own shipment** is allowed: on submit of a Delivery Note / Sales Invoice (update_stock), `SellingController.update_stock_ledger` (`erpnext/controllers/selling_controller.py:676`) first calls `update_reserved_qty` (selling_controller.py:492), which reloads each referenced SO and shrinks `Bin.reserved_qty` by the delivered qty; and `update_stock_reservation_entries` (selling_controller.py:930) matches each item row to its SREs (`voucher_type="Sales Order"`, SO + `so_detail` + warehouse, `delivered_qty < reserved_qty`), raises `sre.delivered_qty` (or per-serial `sb_entries.delivered_qty`), then calls `sre.update_status()` and `sre.update_reserved_stock_in_bin()` — releasing exactly that qty, so the ledger's `reserved_stock` drops and the SLE passes. `StockController.update_stock_reservation_entries` (`erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py:402`) does the equivalent for `transferred_qty`/`consumed_qty` in the subcontracting flow, and `WorkOrderStockReservation` (`erpnext/manufacturing/doctype/work_order/services/reservation.py:54`) does it for work-order material transfers (`transferred_qty`) and consumption (`consumed_qty`). **Key files:** `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reservation_entry/stock_reservation_entry.py` (the SRE doctype + `StockReservation` engine), `erpnext/stock/doctype/bin/bin.py` (`set_projected_qty`, `update_reserved_stock`), `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py` (`get_reserved_qty`, `update_bin_qty`), `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` (`validate_negative_stock`, `validate_reserved_stock`, `validate_reserved_serial_nos`), `erpnext/selling/doctype/sales_order/services/reservation.py` + `erpnext/controllers/selling_controller.py` (record/consume the promise).

final answer
## Where the reverse calculation happens The whole mechanism lives in **`erpnext/controllers/taxes_and_totals.py`**, in the `calculate_taxes_and_totals` class that runs on every Sales/Purchase transaction (SO, Quotation, invoices, DN/PR, POS…). The pipeline is `_calculate()` (line 78): ``` calculate_item_values() → update_item_tax_map() → initialize_taxes() → determine_exclusive_rate() ← the "work backwards" step → calculate_net_total() → calculate_taxes() → adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax() ``` A tax row flagged with **`included_in_print_rate = 1`** (the "Include in Item Rate / Paid Amount" checkbox on the Taxes and Charges child table) means the item's `rate`/`amount` is a gross, tax-inclusive figure. `determine_exclusive_rate()` (line 303) bails out early if no row has that flag; otherwise, for every item row it strips the taxes back out. ## The core math For each item it loops over the tax rows and builds two running values per row: - `tax.tax_fraction_for_current_item` — this tax's rate expressed as a fraction of the net amount. - `tax.grand_total_fraction_for_current_item` — cumulative share of the final gross: `1 + fraction` for the first row, otherwise *previous row's grand_total_fraction + this row's fraction*. It also accumulates `cumulated_tax_fraction` (sum of all inclusive fractions) and `total_inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty` (flat per-unit amounts). Then (lines 329–343): ```python amount = flt(item.amount) - total_inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty item._unrounded_net_amount = amount / (1 + cumulated_tax_fraction) item.net_amount = flt(item._unrounded_net_amount, …) item.net_rate = flt(item.net_amount / item.qty, …) ``` I.e. it inverts `gross = net × (1 + Σfractions) + flat amounts` to `net = (gross − flat) / (1 + Σfractions)`. Example: rate 110 with a single 10% inclusive tax → net = 110 / 1.10 = 100. `calculate_item_values()` (line 224) initially just sets `net_rate = rate` and `net_amount = amount`; `determine_exclusive_rate()` then overwrites those with the pre-tax values. The raw unrounded result is kept on `item._unrounded_net_amount` and reused later in `get_current_tax_and_net_amount()` (lines 609–617) so each inclusive tax amount is computed off the unrounded net, avoiding double rounding across rows. ## How each special case is handled — `get_current_tax_fraction()` (line 348) 1. **Rate resolution per item** — `_get_tax_rate()` (line 384) first looks up the account in the item's `item_tax_rate` JSON (built by `update_item_tax_map()` → `get_item_tax_map()` in `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py` from the Item Tax Template), falling back to `tax.rate`. If the template marks the tax type `not_applicable` (`NOT_APPLICABLE_TAX`), the row contributes zero fraction and is skipped entirely. 2. **Multiple inclusive taxes** — every row with `included_in_print_rate` contributes its own fraction, and all fractions simply add up in `cumulated_tax_fraction`, so the single division strips them all at once. Three 10%/5%/8% inclusive rows → denominator `1.23`. 3. **Compounding rows**: - `charge_type == "On Net Total"` → `fraction = rate/100`. - `"On Previous Row Amount"` → `fraction = (rate/100) × taxes[row_id-1].tax_fraction_for_current_item` — tax on the previous row's *own tax amount* only. - `"On Previous Row Total"` → `fraction = (rate/100) × taxes[row_id-1].grand_total_fraction_for_current_item` — tax on net *plus all preceding inclusive taxes*, i.e. genuine tax-on-tax compounding. (E.g. 10% net + 5% on previous-row-total → fractions 0.10 and 0.055 → denominator 1.155.) The same chain logic is mirrored in the forward pass (`get_current_tax_and_net_amount`, lines 618–623) using `tax_amount_for_current_item` / `grand_total_for_current_item`. 4. **Per-quantity taxes** (`charge_type == "On Item Quantity"`, line 375) — the rate is an absolute amount per unit, not a percentage, so it can't be a fraction. Instead `inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty = flt(tax_rate)`, which is multiplied by `item.qty` into `total_inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty` (line 327) and *subtracted* from the gross amount before the division (line 334) — a hybrid: flat removal first, proportional division second. 5. **Deduction-type taxes** (lines 378–380) — if `tax.add_deduct_tax == "Deduct"` (purchase-side deducted charges), both `current_tax_fraction` and `inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty` are negated (`*= -1.0`). A negative fraction means the reverse division *increases* the net amount — consistent with a deduction reducing the payable total. ## Guardrails and downstream fixes - **Validation** — `validate_inclusive_tax()` in `erpnext/accounts/services/taxes.py` (line 298), invoked from `initialize_taxes()` (line 259), throws if: an "Actual" charge is marked inclusive; an "On Previous Row Amount"/"On Previous Row Total" row references rows that aren't themselves inclusive (all rows before it, for Previous Row Total); or a "Valuation"-category tax is marked inclusive. This guarantees the fraction chain stays algebraically valid. - **Grand-total reconciliation** — `adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax()` (line 700) compares `doc.total + non-inclusive tax amounts` against the last tax row's cumulative `total`; any residual within rounding precision is stored in `self.grand_total_diff` and folded into `grand_total` in `calculate_totals()` (line 731), so the printed grand total equals the sum of the inclusive rates despite per-row rounding. (With Grand-Total discounts, `discount_amount_applied` skips the re-derivation and `apply_discount_amount()` instead distributes the discount proportionally over the already-derived net amounts.) - **Analogous case** — Payment Entry has its own copy of this logic in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py`: `determine_exclusive_rate()` (line 1486) uses `included_in_paid_amount` to back the taxes out of `paid_amount_after_tax = base_paid_amount / (1 + cumulated_tax_fraction)`. - **Printing** — whether taxes are shown hidden/inside the rate is controlled by `AccountsController.is_inclusive_tax()` (`erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py`, line 977) via the `show_inclusive_tax_in_print` Accounts Setting. In short: ERPNext treats each inclusive tax as a fraction of the net amount (chained for compounding), a negative fraction for deductions, and a flat per-unit subtraction for quantity-based taxes, then solves `net = (gross − flat amounts) / (1 + Σ fractions)` per item row in `determine_exclusive_rate()`.

final answer
## Where the backwards computation happens Everything lives in **`erpnext/controllers/taxes_and_totals.py`**, inside the `calculate_taxes_and_totals` class. The pipeline is `_calculate()` (lines 78–89), which runs in this order: 1. `calculate_item_values()` — sets `item.amount = rate × qty` (the tax-**inclusive** amount, since the user's rate includes tax) 2. `initialize_taxes()` — resets per-tax accumulators and runs `validate_inclusive_tax` 3. **`determine_exclusive_rate()` (lines 303–343) — this is the backwards step** 4. `calculate_net_total()`, `calculate_taxes()` (line 418) — recomputes each tax row *forward* off the now-exclusive net amounts via `get_current_tax_and_net_amount()` (line 591) 5. `adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax()` (line 700) and `calculate_totals()` (line 731) — reconcile rounding The identical logic is mirrored client-side in `erpnext/public/js/controllers/taxes_and_totals.js` (same method names, e.g. `adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax()` at line 628) so the UI updates live. ## The backwards math: `determine_exclusive_rate()` If no row in the Taxes table has `included_in_print_rate` set, the function returns immediately. Otherwise, for each item it walks the tax rows in order and, via **`get_current_tax_fraction()` (lines 348–382)**, accumulates two values: - `current_tax_fraction` — how much each *value-based* inclusive tax adds relative to the pre-tax amount (`rate/100` for `On Net Total`) - `inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty` — for *quantity-based* inclusive taxes (see below) It also stores two running fields on each tax row, used by compounding rows: - `tax_fraction_for_current_item` — the row's own effective fraction - `grand_total_fraction_for_current_item` — the cumulative multiplier so far (`1 + Σ previous fractions`; line 318–324) Then the algebraic inversion (lines 329–338): ```python amount = flt(item.amount) - total_inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty item._unrounded_net_amount = amount / (1 + cumulated_tax_fraction) ``` Because the inclusive price satisfies `amount = net × (1 + Σ fractions) + Σ (per-qty taxes × qty)`, solving for `net` gives the pre-tax line amount. Both `item.net_amount` and `item.net_rate` are set from it, and `_unrounded_net_amount` is deliberately kept unrounded so the forward pass doesn't compound rounding errors. The per-item rate actually used is resolved by `_get_tax_rate()` (line 384) from the item's Item Tax Template map (`item.item_tax_rate` JSON); a rate of `NOT_APPLICABLE_TAX` (`"N/A"`, defined in `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py`) makes `get_current_tax_fraction` return 0 — that tax simply doesn't exist for the item and is excluded from the divisor. ## How each special case is handled **Multiple inclusive taxes.** Every inclusive row contributes its own fraction to `cumulated_tax_fraction`, and one single division by `(1 + Σ fractions)` produces a pre-tax base consistent with *all* of them at once. In the forward pass (`get_current_tax_and_net_amount`, lines 605–617), each inclusive `On Net Total` row then computes `current_tax_amount = (rate/100) × item._unrounded_net_amount` — using the unrounded net specifically to avoid double rounding. Non-inclusive rows contribute 0 to the fraction and are charged on top afterwards, as usual. **Compounding tax rows (tax on tax).** - `On Previous Row Amount` (line 365–368): fraction = `(rate/100) × taxes[row_id-1].tax_fraction_for_current_item` — a percentage of the *previous tax's* effective fraction, i.e. tax on that tax. - `On Previous Row Total` (line 370–373): fraction = `(rate/100) × taxes[row_id-1].grand_total_fraction_for_current_item` — a percentage of the running cumulative multiplier (item value plus all previous inclusive taxes). These stacked fractions still just sum into `cumulated_tax_fraction`, so one division by `(1 + Σ)` lands on the correct pre-tax base regardless of chaining depth. Validity is enforced by `validate_inclusive_tax` in **`erpnext/accounts/services/taxes.py` (lines 298–322)** and its JS twin `erpnext/public/js/controllers/accounts.js::validate_inclusive_tax` (lines 191–231): an `Actual` charge type can never be inclusive; an `On Previous Row Amount` row's referenced row must itself be inclusive; an `On Previous Row Total` row requires *all* rows above it to be inclusive; and `category == "Valuation"` rows can't be inclusive. **Per-quantity taxes (`On Item Quantity`).** These can't be a fraction of value, so `get_current_tax_fraction` returns `inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty = flt(tax_rate)` instead (line 375–376). In `determine_exclusive_rate`, this is multiplied by `item.qty` (line 327) and **subtracted from `item.amount` before the division** — so flat per-unit taxes come out of the inclusive total first, and the percentage division handles the rest. In the forward pass (line 624–626), the tax is recomputed exactly as `rate × qty`, with `current_net_amount` left at 0 (the taxable-base concept doesn't apply). **Deduction-type taxes (`add_deduct_tax == "Deduct"`, e.g. TDS on purchase docs).** Lines 378–380 of `get_current_tax_fraction` negate both the fraction and the per-qty amount, so a deducted inclusive tax *subtracts* from `(1 + Σ fractions)` — raising the computed pre-tax base, which is consistent with a tax that is withheld from the payable total yet still baked into the printed rate. Downstream, `get_tax_amount_if_for_valuation_or_deduction()` (lines 568–580) zeroes out `Valuation`-category taxes from document totals and multiplies `Deduct` taxes by −1 when accumulating cumulative totals on purchase documents. ## Closing the loop on rounding Because net amounts are rounded to field precision, the forward pass may not perfectly reproduce the original inclusive total. `adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax()` compares `doc.total + non_inclusive_tax_amount` against the last tax row's cumulative `total` (minus any applied discount); if the difference is within rounding tolerance (`5.0 / 10 ** tax_precision`), it's kept as `grand_total_diff`, which `calculate_totals()` (lines 731–745) adds to `grand_total` while excluding it from `total_taxes_and_charges` — so the printed grand total equals what the customer actually pays and inclusive taxes are never double-counted. Item-level rounding drift is absorbed separately in `set_item_wise_tax()` (lines 633–671, cumulative-delta error diffusion) and `adjust_rounding_in_item_wise_tax_details()`. (There's also a print-side flag: `AccountsController.is_inclusive_tax()` in `erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py` (lines 977–985) checks Accounts Settings' `show_inclusive_tax_in_print` to decide how inclusive taxes are displayed on the printed document — display only, not calculation.)

final answer
I have the complete picture. Here's how ERPNext handles tax-inclusive item pricing. ## Overview ERPNext doesn't store a "price includes tax" flag on the Item Price itself. Instead, each row in a document's **Taxes and Charges** table carries the **`included_in_print_rate`** checkbox ("Include in Print Rate", coming from the Sales/Purchase Taxes and Charges Template). When any row has it set, `item.rate` (and `price_list_rate`) is treated as the *gross, tax-inclusive* amount, and the pre-tax values (`net_rate`, `net_amount`) are derived by reversing the tax math. Everything happens in **`erpnext/controllers/taxes_and_totals.py`**, class `calculate_taxes_and_totals`, in the `_calculate()` pipeline (L78–89): ``` calculate_item_values() # amount = rate × qty (gross, tax-inclusive) initialize_taxes() # resets fraction fields; validates inclusive config determine_exclusive_rate() # ← the "work backwards" step (L303) calculate_net_total() calculate_taxes() # forward pass: assigns each tax amount per item adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax() # keeps grand total == what customer pays calculate_totals() ``` ## The backwards step: `determine_exclusive_rate()` (L303–343) It early-returns unless `any(cint(tax.included_in_print_rate) ...)`. Otherwise, for **each item row** it walks the tax table **top to bottom once** and builds two accumulators via `get_current_tax_fraction()`: - `cumulated_tax_fraction` — the sum of all ad-valorem inclusive rates, expressed as fractions of the *net* amount (a 10% tax contributes `0.10`, not `10/110`). - `total_inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty` — absolute per-unit inclusive taxes (accumulated as `inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty * item.qty`). Then it solves one closed-form equation per line: ```python amount = flt(item.amount) - total_inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty item._unrounded_net_amount = amount / (1 + cumulated_tax_fraction) item.net_amount = flt(item._unrounded_net_amount, ...) item.net_rate = flt(item.net_amount / item.qty, ...) ``` i.e. **net = (gross − fixed per-qty inclusive taxes) ÷ (1 + Σfractions)**. Because the whole chain is collapsed into a single divisor, multiple inclusive taxes are solved simultaneously — no iteration is needed. Note it is skipped when `discount_amount_applied` (discount-on-Grand-Total path handles gross separately) or when `qty` is 0. ## How each tax configuration contributes — `get_current_tax_fraction()` (L348–382) Only rows flagged `included_in_print_rate` contribute a fraction; non-inclusive rows contribute 0 and are simply added on top later. The effective rate per item comes from `_get_tax_rate()` (L384–391): the item's **Item Tax Template** map (`item.item_tax_rate` JSON) overrides `tax.rate`; a template entry of `"N/A"` (`NOT_APPLICABLE_TAX`, defined in `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py` L41) makes that tax contribute **nothing** for that item — so the gross is backed out using only the taxes actually applicable to that item. Per charge type: | Charge type | Contribution to the backwards math | |---|---| | **On Net Total** | `fraction = rate / 100` | | **On Previous Row Amount** (compounding on one tax) | `fraction = (rate/100) × taxes[row_id−1].tax_fraction_for_current_item` — i.e. rate applied to the *referenced tax's own fraction* | | **On Previous Row Total** (compounding on everything above) | `fraction = (rate/100) × taxes[row_id−1].grand_total_fraction_for_current_item`, where each row's `grand_total_fraction_for_current_item` is a running sum seeded as `1 + fraction` for row 0 and `previous_grand_total_fraction + fraction` thereafter | | **On Item Quantity** (fixed per unit) | no fraction; `inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty = flt(tax_rate)` | | **Deduct** rows (purchase-side `add_deduct_tax == "Deduct"`) | both the fraction and the per-qty amount are multiplied by **−1** | **Compounding example** (verified against `test_inclusive_tax_with_decimal_value_on_previous_row_total` in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/sales_invoice/test_sales_invoice.py` L612–646): 10% inclusive + 5% "On Previous Row Total" inclusive → fraction = 0.10 + 0.05×1.10 = 0.155 → net = 50,000.55 / 1.155 = **43,290.52**, and the grand total stays exactly 50,000.55. Similarly the "On Previous Row Amount" test (L539–573) yields 0.10 + 0.05×0.10 = 0.105 → divide by 1.105. **Mixed percentage + per-quantity**: because the fixed per-qty amount is *subtracted from the gross first* and only then divided by `(1 + Σfractions)`, a line can carry both an inclusive VAT and an inclusive per-unit excise (e.g. per litre) and still resolve in one division. **Deduction-type inclusive rows**: the sign flip means such a tax *lowers* the total; in the backwards equation it reduces the divisor (and its per-qty equivalent adds back), so the extracted net is correspondingly larger — later, `calculate_taxes` emits a negative tax amount. In `set_item_wise_tax()` (L633–671) the item-wise breakup applies `multiplier = -1` for Deduct rows as well. ## Consistency guards 1. **Validation** — `validate_inclusive_tax()` in `erpnext/accounts/services/taxes.py` (L298–322), invoked from `initialize_taxes()`: an inclusive row cannot be charge type "Actual"; "On Previous Row Amount" requires the referenced row to also be inclusive; "On Previous Row Total" requires **all** preceding rows to be inclusive (since its fraction rides on the running total); "Valuation"-category charges can never be inclusive (they don't hit the bill). 2. **Forward pass uses the unrounded net** — in `get_current_tax_and_net_amount()` (L609–615), inclusive "On Net Total" taxes compute `tax_amount = (rate/100) × item._unrounded_net_amount` rather than the rounded `net_amount`, so `net + Σtax` reproduces the exact gross typed by the user (the decimal-value tests above depend on this — e.g. 45,249.37 + 4,524.94 + 226.25 = 50,000.55 wait, precisely: taxes 4,524.94 + 226.25 + net 45,249.37 ≈ 50,000.55 ✓). 3. **Grand total preservation** — `adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax()` (L700–729) computes `diff = doc.total + non_inclusive_tax_amount − last_tax.total`. If it's within rounding tolerance (≤ 0.5 unit of the last tax's precision) it's kept as `grand_total_diff` and folded in by `calculate_totals()` (L731–745), so the customer still pays exactly the gross amount; `total_taxes_and_charges = grand_total − net_total − diff`. Valuation-only rows are excluded from this sum by `get_tax_amount_if_for_valuation_or_deduction()` (L568). 4. **Discounts** — with discount on Net Total, `apply_discount_amount()` (L857+) redistributes the discount proportionally over the *already-extracted* `net_amount`s; with `apply_discount_on = "Grand Total"` and a cash/non-trade discount, `discount_amount_applied` is set and `determine_exclusive_rate` is bypassed since the gross was already reduced. ## Net effect The user-facing fields (`rate`, `amount`, printed amounts, grand total) remain tax-inclusive, while the pre-tax values (`net_rate`, `net_amount`, `base_net_rate`, `base_net_amount`) — which feed GL entries, stock valuation and tax reporting — are the result of the single closed-form division in `determine_exclusive_rate()`, with per-row tax amounts then recomputed forward in `calculate_taxes()` so every row's contribution is individually auditable in the item-wise tax breakup.

final answer
## Where it happens The reverse ("backward") computation lives in **`erpnext/controllers/taxes_and_totals.py`**, in the `TaxesAndTotals` class that every selling/buying document uses: - `calculate()` (line 46) → `_calculate()` (line 78), whose pipeline is: `calculate_item_values()` → `update_item_tax_map()` → `initialize_taxes()` → **`determine_exclusive_rate()`** (line 303) → `calculate_net_total()` → `calculate_taxes()` → `adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax()` (line 700) → `calculate_totals()` - The helper that classifies each tax row: **`get_current_tax_fraction()`** (line 348), with per-item rate lookup in `_get_tax_rate()` (line 384). - The same math is mirrored client-side for live on-screen recalculation in **`erpnext/public/js/controllers/taxes_and_totals.js`** (`determine_exclusive_rate()` line 254, `get_current_tax_fraction()` line 300). ## The core idea 1. `calculate_item_values()` (line 224) first treats the entered rate as the full customer-facing (tax-inclusive) amount: `item.amount = rate × qty`, `net_rate = rate`, `net_amount = amount`, `item_tax_amount = 0`. 2. `determine_exclusive_rate()` returns immediately unless **any** tax row has `included_in_print_rate` checked (line 304). 3. For each item it loads `item.item_tax_rate` — a JSON map of `account_head → rate` produced by `update_item_tax_map()` → `get_item_tax_map()` (`erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:885`), which merges the document's tax rows with the selected **Item Tax Template** (template rates win; `"N/A"` marks a tax as not applicable to that item). 4. Each inclusive tax row contributes a *fraction* of the pre-tax amount, and the pre-tax base is algebraically inverted: ```python item._unrounded_net_amount = (item.amount − total_inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty) / (1 + cumulated_tax_fraction) ``` (lines 334–338), then `net_amount`, `net_rate = net_amount / qty`, and their `base_*` company-currency copies are set. Keeping `_unrounded_net_amount` matters later: `calculate_taxes()` uses it for inclusive "On Net Total" rows (lines 609–615) to avoid double rounding. ## How each tax shape is handled (get_current_tax_fraction, lines 348–382) - **Multiple inclusive taxes:** every row with `included_in_print_rate` contributes to `cumulated_tax_fraction`; row 0 gets `grand_total_fraction_for_current_item = 1 + fraction`, row *i* gets the previous row's fraction **plus** its own — a running `(1 + r1 + r2 + …)` that later rows compound on. - **Compounding rows** (`charge_type = "On Previous Row Amount"` / `"On Previous Row Total"`): the fraction is `(rate/100) × previous row's tax_fraction_for_current_item` or `× previous row's grand_total_fraction_for_current_item` respectively — so a tax computed on the amount/total *including* earlier inclusive taxes is correctly folded into the division denominator. Validation lives in `validate_inclusive_tax()` (`erpnext/accounts/services/taxes.py:298`, invoked from `initialize_taxes()` line 259): an "Actual" tax can never be inclusive, an "On Previous Row Amount" must reference an inclusive row, "On Previous Row Total" requires **all** preceding rows to be inclusive, and "Valuation"-category taxes can't be inclusive. If the item's template marks the account `"N/A"`, the row contributes zero fraction for that item (line 359). - **Per-quantity taxes** (`charge_type = "On Item Quantity"`): a rate per unit can't be expressed as a percentage of the base, so it goes into `inclusive_tax_amount_per_qty = flt(tax_rate)`, which is multiplied by `item.qty` and **subtracted** from `item.amount` before the percentage division (line 327, 334). Forward pass symmetric: `get_current_tax_and_net_amount()` computes `tax_amount = rate × qty` (line 624–626) and `set_item_wise_tax()` (line 633) records no taxable amount for these rows. - **Deduction-type taxes** (`add_deduct_tax == "Deduct"`): both the fraction and the per-qty amount are **negated** (lines 378–380; JS lines 328–331), so a deduct-inclusive tax reduces the cumulative denominator — effectively shrinking the tax bundle assumed inside the rate. The same −1 multiplier is applied when storing item-wise tax amounts (line 635) and when reconciling item-wise rounding (line 542). ## Closing the loop so totals stay honest After the reversal, `calculate_taxes()` (line 418) runs the normal forward pass over the now-exclusive net amounts, and `adjust_grand_total_for_inclusive_tax()` (line 700) checks that `doc.total + non-inclusive taxes` matches the last tax row's cumulative `total`; any residual within rounding precision becomes `grand_total_diff` (line 721–729), which `calculate_totals()` (line 731) uses so that `grand_total` stays exactly what the customer pays (the sum of the tax-inclusive rates) and `total_taxes_and_charges = grand_total − net_total − grand_total_diff`. Note this whole stage is skipped when a grand-total discount is being applied (`discount_amount_applied`) — net amounts are then recomputed separately, and rounding differences in item-wise tax details are diffused onto the last item row by `adjust_rounding_in_item_wise_tax_details()` (line 514).

Here's the complete answer. ## The holding spot: **"Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRBNB)** The value of received-but-unbilled goods is parked in the company-level account `stock_received_but_not_billed` — created as a **Liability**-root account with `account_type = "Stock Received But Not Billed"` (`erpnext/setup/doctype/company/company.js:338-341`, default set in `set_default_accounts` in `erpnext/setup/doctype/company/company.py:704`, only when `enable_perpetual_inventory`). The fixed-asset analogue is `asset_received_but_not_billed`. It is a suspense liability: goods are in stock, but no supplier payable exists yet. ## Receipt side — Purchase Receipt *credits* SRBNB **File:** `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/purchase_receipt.py` + `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py` 1. `StockController.make_gl_entries` (`erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py:178`) sees a submitted PR and calls `PurchaseReceipt.get_gl_entries` (`purchase_receipt.py:478-483`) → `PurchaseReceiptGLComposer.compose` (`gl_composer.py:23`). 2. In `_make_item_gl_entries` (`gl_composer.py:39`), for each stock item the holding account is resolved at lines 297-301: ```python stock_asset_rbnb = doc.get_company_default("asset_received_but_not_billed") # fixed asset else doc.get_company_default("stock_received_but_not_billed") ``` 3. Two paired entries are built per item: - `make_item_asset_inward_gl_entry` (line 57): **Debit** the warehouse's inventory account with `stock_value_diff`, taken from the Stock Ledger Entry via `get_stock_value_difference` (`purchase_receipt.py:544`). - `make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry` (line 74): **Credit** SRBNB (implemented as a *negative debit* with `against_account=stock_asset_account_name`) for `item.base_net_amount`. Net: `Dr Stock-in-Hand / Cr Stock Received But Not Billed`. `_make_tax_gl_entries` (line 394) additionally credits valuation-tax accounts capitalized via `item.item_tax_amount`. **Creditors is never touched** — no bill, no payable. ## Billing side — Purchase Invoice *debits* SRBNB back out **File:** `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/purchase_invoice.py` + `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py` + `.../services/expense_account.py` 1. **Account resolution:** `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (`expense_account.py:20`, called from `PurchaseInvoice.validate` at `purchase_invoice.py:288-291`). For a stock item linked to a receipt (`item.purchase_receipt`), it checks whether SRBNB was actually credited in that PR (`frappe.db.exists("GL Entry", {voucher_type: "Purchase Receipt", voucher_no: item.purchase_receipt, account: stock_not_billed_account})`, lines 57-65) and then **forces `item.expense_account = stock_not_billed_account`** (line 82). If no PR exists yet, the same account is used so the invoice can precede the receipt. 2. **GL posting:** `PurchaseInvoice.get_gl_entries` (`purchase_invoice.py:703-708`) → `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.compose` (`gl_composer.py:18`): - `make_supplier_gl_entry` (line 80) **credits `credit_to` (Creditors)** with the grand total. - `make_item_gl_entries` (line 129), in the non-`update_stock` branch (lines 319-350), **debits `item.expense_account` — i.e., SRBNB — against the supplier**. The code comment states it explicitly: *"the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock… Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount against the supplier."* Net effect of the two documents combined: `Dr Inventory / Cr Creditors`, and the SRBNB suspense balance nets to zero — the value has moved out of the holding spot into a real payable. 3. **Valuation taxes:** if the PR didn't book them (checked via the GL lookup at lines 402-411, the invoice-before-receipt case), the PI debits SRBNB for `item.item_tax_amount` and accumulates `doc.negative_expense_to_be_booked` (line 437); `make_tax_gl_entries` (line 605) then credits the tax accounts to square it off. 4. **Status sync:** `BillingStatusService.update_billing_status_in_pr` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/billing_status.py:21`) writes `billed_amt` back to `Purchase Receipt Item` and calls `update_billing_percentage` (from `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/billing_status.py`), advancing the PR from "To Bill" toward completed. ## Edge cases handled by the same machinery - **Invoice first, receipt later:** PI debits SRBNB; the PR's later credit offsets it. - **`update_stock` PI (no PR):** `set_expense_account` instead points `expense_account` at the warehouse inventory account (`expense_account.py:51-54`), so the composer debits inventory directly — SRBNB is bypassed. - **Rate discrepancies at billing time:** flow back to the PR as `item.amount_difference_with_purchase_invoice`, adjusted against SRBNB by `make_amount_difference_entry` (`gl_composer.py:202`), and exchange-rate differences produce matched SRBNB/`exchange_gain_loss_account` entries in both composers (PR `gl_composer.py:126-162`, PI `gl_composer.py:352-393` via `get_purchase_document_details`). - **Internal transfers:** `make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry` swaps SRBNB for the supplier-warehouse inventory account when `item.from_warehouse` is set (`gl_composer.py:84-87`). Both sides are pinned by tests: PR credits SRBNB 500 (`test_purchase_receipt.py:369`), the matching PI debits SRBNB 500 / credits Creditors 720 (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/test_purchase_invoice.py:329-342`, `test_gl_entries_with_perpetual_inventory_against_pr`).
