I have the full picture now. Here's the complete answer. ## Context (perpetual inventory enabled, Standard Cost item) Example used throughout: item valued at **standard rate 130**, received on a Purchase Receipt at **actual rate 200** (variance = 70). ### What the Purchase Receipt already posted (the baseline) In `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py`, for a stock item with perpetual inventory: 1. `make_item_asset_inward_gl_entry` — **Dr Warehouse inventory account 130** (the `stock_value_difference` from the Stock Ledger, valued at the standard rate from `get_item_standard_rate()` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py`). 2. `make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry` — **Cr "Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRBNB) 200** (the actual receipt amount, `item.base_net_amount`). 3. `make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` — the gap (200 − 130 = 70) goes to `get_divisional_loss_account()`, which for `get_valuation_method(item) == "Standard Cost"` returns `get_purchase_price_variance_account(item, company)` (Item Default `purchase_price_variance_account`, else Company `default_purchase_price_variance_account`) — **Dr Purchase Price Variance 70**, against the stock account. Verified by `test_pr_books_variance_to_ppv_account` (PPV = 70, default COGS = 0). ## Purchase Invoice with Update Stock OFF (against that PR) **Expense-account resolution** — `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account()` in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py`: since the item is a stock item, `is_opening == "No"`, not fixed-asset/drop-ship, and `doc.update_stock` is falsy, it checks that the PR actually credited SRBNB (GL Entry lookup on voucher_type=Purchase Receipt) and **forces `item.expense_account = "Stock Received But Not Billed"`** (msgprint "Expense Head Changed" on validate). **GL composition** — `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries()` in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`, the non-update-stock `else` branch posts exactly one debit per item: - **Dr SRBNB 200 / Cr Supplier 200** (`base_net_amount` via `TaxService.get_amount_and_base_amount(item, None)`), against the supplier. The code comment spells out the design: *"the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock (at standard) and the Purchase Price Variance. Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount against the supplier — booking PPV again would double count it and leave SRBNB partially uncleared."* So the invoice's expense side is a single debit to the **interim liability SRBNB at the full billed value (200)**; the **PPV account is not touched at all**. This is asserted by `test_pi_without_update_stock_does_not_rebook_variance` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/test_item_standard_cost.py`: `booked(ppv_account) == 0`, `booked(srbnb_account) == 200`. Minor extras in this branch: if the item carries valuation-tax `item_tax_amount` that the PR did *not* already book, an additional Dr SRBNB for that amount is posted with the tax accounts credited (`negative_expense_to_be_booked` logic in `make_item_gl_entries`/`make_tax_gl_entries`); an exchange-rate discrepancy entry (Dr expense/SRBNB, Cr exchange gain/loss) can also fire when the PR's conversion rate differed. ## Purchase Invoice with Update Stock ON Here the invoice does the stock movement itself, so the accounting is materially different: 1. `set_expense_account()` sets `item.expense_account` to the **warehouse's inventory account** (via `get_inventory_account_map()`), not SRBNB. 2. In `make_item_gl_entries()`, `make_stock_adjustment_entry()` first compares the invoice value (`valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor` = 200) with the PI's own SLE `stock_value_difference` (standard cost = 130). Because they differ, it posts a **"Stock Adjustment" entry: Dr Purchase Price Variance account 70**, against `item.expense_account` — `get_stock_variance_account()` returns `get_purchase_price_variance_account()` for Standard Cost items (vs. Company `default_expense_account` for other items). It then resets `warehouse_debit_amount = 130`. 3. The main item entry then posts **Dr Warehouse inventory account 130 / Cr Supplier 200** ("Accounting Entry for Stock"). Net effect: **Dr Inventory 130 + Dr Purchase Price Variance 70 = Cr Supplier 200** — the invoice capitalizes stock at standard cost and books the variance itself; SRBNB is never used. ## The difference in one line - **Update Stock OFF (against a PR):** expense side = one debit to **"Stock Received But Not Billed" at the full billed amount (200)** — pure liability clearance; the standard-cost variance (70) was already recognized on the PR and is deliberately **not re-booked**. - **Update Stock ON:** expense side = two debits — **the warehouse inventory account at standard cost (130)** plus the **Purchase Price Variance account for the gap (70)** — because the invoice owns the stock valuation and must recognize the variance itself.

All the pieces are confirmed. Here's the complete picture. ## Setting: perpetual inventory + Standard Cost item With **perpetual inventory** enabled (`erpnext.is_perpetual_inventory_enabled`) and an item whose valuation method resolves to `"Standard Cost"` (`erpnext/stock/utils.py:350` `get_valuation_method` — Item → Company → Stock Settings), the stock ledger values every inward movement at the item's standard rate from the **Item Standard Cost** record (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:2245-2254` uses `get_item_standard_rate`). So the **Purchase Receipt** (via `PurchaseReceiptGLComposer._make_item_gl_entries`, `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py:275-335`) has already posted, at receipt time: - **Dr** warehouse Stock account — `stock_value_diff` = the SLE stock value = qty × **standard cost** (line 309) - **Cr** "Stock Received But Not Billed" — the full document value (`base_net_amount`, lines 74-124) - **Dr** Purchase Price Variance account — the gap between document value and standard stock value, posted by `make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` (lines 233-273) through `get_divisional_loss_account` (lines 370-392) → `get_purchase_price_variance_account` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py:334-353`: per-company Item Default override, else Company default `default_purchase_price_variance_account`) ## Purchase Invoice against that PR, Update Stock OFF First, this is the **only** combination allowed: `PurchaseInvoice.validate` → `validate_purchase_receipt_if_update_stock` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/purchase_invoice.py:299, 586-595`) throws *"Stock cannot be updated ... because a Purchase Receipt ... has already been created"* if `update_stock` is checked on a PR-linked row. 1. **Expense head is forced to SRBNB.** `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py:20-102`) checks whether the linked PR credited "Stock Received But Not Billed" (`negative_expense_booked_in_pr`, lines 56-82) and sets `item.expense_account = stock_not_billed_account` — it even warns if the user picked a different head ("Expense Head changed to … because expense is booked against this account in Purchase Receipt …"). 2. **The invoice posts exactly one expense-side entry.** In `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.compose` → `make_item_gl_entries` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py:129-350`), the non-stock-update branch (lines 319-350) posts: - **Dr "Stock Received But Not Billed" = the item's full `base_net_amount` (billed value at invoice rate), against Supplier** (lines 337-350) - plus the supplier credit (grand total, `add_supplier_gl_entry`, lines 80-127) The code comment (lines 332-336) states the design explicitly: *"the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock (at standard) and the Purchase Price Variance. Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount against the supplier — booking PPV again would double count it and leave SRBNB partially uncleared."* So: **no Stock account entry, no PPV entry, no Stock Ledger movement from the invoice.** The variance (receipt/billed rate vs standard cost) was already absorbed by the PR's PPV debit. Ancillary entries only: an exchange-rate-discrepancy pair (Dr expense account / Cr exchange gain-loss, lines 352-393) if the PI conversion rate changed vs the PR, and a reverse-SRBNB debit for `item_tax_amount` of valuation taxes the PR didn't book (lines 395-439 + `make_tax_gl_entries`, lines 650-680). If Buying Settings `set_landed_cost_based_on_purchase_invoice_rate` is on, `update_billing_percentage(adjust_incoming_rate=True)` → `adjust_incoming_rate_for_pr` (`.../purchase_receipt/services/billing_status.py:47-55, 281-282, 361-370`) reposts the PR so its SRBNB credit and PPV split realign to the billed amount — which is what lets the invoice's single SRBNB debit clear the account fully. With standard 100 / billed 120: PR posted Dr Stock 100, Dr PPV 20, Cr SRBNB 120; the invoice posts Dr SRBNB 120 → SRBNB nets to zero. ## Same invoice with Update Stock enabled (i.e., no linked PR) This mode is mutually exclusive with PR billing, and the GL structure is different: 1. `set_expense_account` (expense_account.py:51-54) sets `item.expense_account` to the **item warehouse's inventory account** (Stock / Stock In Hand) — SRBNB is not used at all. 2. `make_item_gl_entries` stock branch (gl_composer.py:180-269) first runs `make_stock_adjustment_entry` (lines 535-603): it compares `warehouse_debit_amount` (invoice valuation = `valuation_rate × qty`) with the invoice's own SLE `stock_value_difference` — which is at **standard cost** for a Standard Cost item. On a mismatch it posts **Dr Purchase Price Variance account** (resolved by `get_stock_variance_account`, lines 523-533 — same PPV account, remark "Stock Adjustment"), against the warehouse account, then clamps `warehouse_debit_amount` back to the SLE (standard) value. 3. It then debits `item.expense_account` — the **Stock account** — for that (standard) amount against Supplier (lines 250-269). The invoice itself creates the stock ledger entries (`update_stock_ledger`, purchase_invoice.py:633-641, 744-750). With standard 100 / billed 120, the stock-updating invoice's expense side is: **Dr Stock account 100 + Dr PPV 20 = 120**, against Supplier — variance and stock value are booked inside the invoice voucher, and SRBNB never appears. ## The difference in one line - **Update Stock off (against PR):** the invoice's expense side is *only* a debit to **"Stock Received But Not Billed"** for the full billed amount; stock and the purchase price variance stay untouched because the PR already booked Stock at standard cost and PPV — the invoice is purely a SRBNB-clearing/supplier-liability document. - **Update Stock on (no PR):** the expense side debit goes to the **warehouse Stock account itself** (not SRBNB), sized at the standard-cost stock value, with a separate **Purchase Price Variance** debit for the invoice-rate-vs-standard difference produced by `make_stock_adjustment_entry`.

I now have the complete picture, confirmed by code and the regression tests. Here's the full answer. ## Setup: what a Standard Cost item's Purchase Receipt already booked For an item with `valuation_method = "Standard Cost"`, the stock ledger forces valuation to the `Item Standard Cost` rate — `process_standard_cost()` in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` (L970–991) overwrites `sle.incoming_rate` with `get_item_standard_rate(...)` for every inward entry. So when the PR is submitted, `PurchaseReceiptGLComposer` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py`) books three entries per item: 1. **Dr warehouse Stock account** at the standard value (`make_item_asset_inward_gl_entry`, debit = SLE `stock_value_diff`, L57–72 / L308–310) 2. **Cr "Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRBNB)** at the *billed/receipt* value (`make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry`, L74–124) 3. **Dr Purchase Price Variance account** for the difference between billed value and standard stock value (`make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` → `get_divisional_loss_account`, L233–273 / L370–392, which routes Standard Cost items to `get_purchase_price_variance_account()` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py` L334; other items get `default_expense_account` instead) Example used in the tests (`test_item_standard_cost.py`): standard rate 130, received @ 200 → PR posts Dr Stock 130, Dr PPV 70, Cr SRBNB 200. ## Purchase Invoice with Update Stock OFF (billed against the PR) `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries()` takes the **else branch (L319–350)** of `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`: - `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account()` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py` L41–82) sees a stock item with `purchase_receipt` set and checks the PR actually credited the company's `stock_received_but_not_billed` account (GL Entry lookup, L57–65); since it did, it **forces `item.expense_account = "Stock Received But Not Billed"`**. - The invoice then posts exactly **one expense-side entry: Dr "Stock Received But Not Billed" for the full billed `base_net_amount`, against the supplier** — the paired entry being **Cr Creditors (`credit_to`) for the grand total** (`add_supplier_gl_entry`, with `against_expense_account` = "Stock Received But Not Billed" built by `set_against_expense_account()`, L164–171). - **No stock-account entry and no PPV entry.** The in-code comment (L332–336) states why: *"the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock (at standard) and the Purchase Price Variance. Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount… booking PPV again would double count it."* The PR's temporary SRBNB credit is what the invoice settles. - (Secondary: if the PI's conversion rate differs from the PR's, an extra expense-account debit vs `exchange_gain_loss_account` credit is posted, L352–393; if the PR didn't book valuation taxes, SRBNB is also debited for `item_tax_amount` with credit to the tax accounts, L395–439.) This is pinned by `test_pi_without_update_stock_does_not_rebook_variance` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/test_item_standard_cost.py` L794–825): PI against that PR (update_stock = 0) asserts `booked(ppv_account) == 0` and `booked(srbnb_account) == 200`. ## Purchase Invoice with Update Stock ON `set_expense_account()` instead sets `item.expense_account` to the item's **warehouse inventory account** (`get_inventory_account_map`/`get_inventory_account_dict`, `erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py` L138–176) — expense_account.py L51–54. In `make_item_gl_entries()`'s update-stock branch (L180–269): - `make_stock_adjustment_entry()` (L535–603) computes `warehouse_debit_amount = valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor` — and `update_valuation_rate()` (`erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py` L414–490) sets `valuation_rate` from the **billed** rate (net rate + valuation taxes), not the standard rate. - The SLE it just created valued stock at the **standard** rate (`stock_value_difference` = 130), so the mismatch triggers a **Dr "Purchase Price Variance" entry** (remarks "Stock Adjustment") via `get_stock_variance_account()` (gl_composer.py L523–533 → PPV account for Standard Cost items), and the stock account is then debited at the standard value. - Result: **Dr Stock account 130 + Dr PPV 70 (= billed − standard) → Cr Creditors 200** (against the stock account, via `add_supplier_gl_entry`). ## The difference in one line With Update Stock off, the invoice's expense side is a single debit to **"Stock Received But Not Billed" at the full billed amount** — it merely clears the temporary liability the PR raised and re-books neither stock nor variance; with Update Stock on, the invoice performs the receipt's accounting itself: the expense-side debit goes to the **warehouse Stock account at the standard value**, with a separate **Purchase Price Variance debit for the billed-vs-standard difference**, so SRBNB is never involved.

## Short answer With **Update Stock off** and a linked Purchase Receipt, the invoice's item-side debit goes **entirely to "Stock Received But Not Billed"** (the liability-clearing account) at the billed amount — it does **not** touch the item's expense/PPV account again, because the Purchase Receipt already booked the stock at standard cost *and* the Purchase Price Variance. With **Update Stock on**, the invoice books the receipt itself: the debit goes to the **warehouse inventory (stock asset) account at standard cost, plus a separate Purchase Price Variance debit** for the billed-vs-standard difference. ## What the Purchase Receipt already booked (context) `PurchaseReceiptGLComposer._make_item_gl_entries` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py:39`, loop at 275–335) posts three entries per stock row: 1. **Debit warehouse inventory account** at `stock_value_diff` — the SLE value, i.e. standard rate × qty (`make_item_asset_inward_gl_entry`, lines 57–72; `stock_value_diff` from `get_stock_value_difference`, line 309). 2. **Credit Stock Received But Not Billed** (company default `stock_received_but_not_billed`) at `base_net_amount` — the billed/receipt rate (`make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry`, lines 74–164). 3. The gap (billed value − standard stock value) via `make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` (233–273) to `get_divisional_loss_account` (370–392) — which for a Standard Cost item is the **Purchase Price Variance account**, resolved by `get_purchase_price_variance_account()` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py:334` (Item Default per company, else Company default `default_purchase_price_variance_account`). ## Invoice with Update Stock OFF (against that PR) **Account resolution** — `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account()` in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py:20`. For a stock item (not fixed asset, not drop-ship, not opening), it checks whether the PR actually credited SRBNB: ```python negative_expense_booked_in_pr = frappe.db.exists( "GL Entry", {"voucher_type": "Purchase Receipt", "voucher_no": item.purchase_receipt, "account": stock_not_billed_account}) if negative_expense_booked_in_pr: ... item.expense_account = stock_not_billed_account # line 82 ``` It even msgprints *"Row {0}: Expense Head changed to {1} because expense is booked against this account in Purchase Receipt {2}"* if the row carried a different expense head. **GL posting** — `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries()` in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py:129`, the non-`update_stock` `else` branch (319–350), posts a single debit: - **Debit `Stock Received But Not Billed`** (`item.expense_account`) with the full billed net amount (`base_amount` via `TaxService.get_amount_and_base_amount`), **against the Supplier**. - The inline comment (lines 332–336) states the design intent verbatim: *"When Update Stock is disabled, this invoice has no stock impact: the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock (at standard) and the Purchase Price Variance. Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount against the supplier — booking PPV again would double count it and leave SRBNB partially uncleared."* So the full invoice picture: Credit Accounts Payable (`credit_to`, grand total, `make_supplier_gl_entry` lines 80–124) ↔ Debit SRBNB per item. Secondary entries only: an exchange-rate discrepancy pair (352–393) if the PR was booked at a different conversion rate, and the valuation-tax/SRBNB reversal (395–439). **No PPV entry, no stock-asset entry, and no Stock Ledger Entries.** (If the PR had *not* credited SRBNB, the expense account would stay as fetched on the row instead of being forced to SRBNB.) ## Invoice with Update Stock ON **Account resolution** — the same `set_expense_account()` overwrites the expense head with the warehouse account first (`expense_account.py:51–54`): `if doc.update_stock and item.warehouse and (not item.from_warehouse): item.expense_account = _inv_dict["account"]` (destination warehouse inventory account from `get_inventory_account_map()`). **GL posting** — the `update_stock` branch of `make_item_gl_entries` (gl_composer.py:180–269): 1. `make_stock_adjustment_entry()` (535–603) computes `warehouse_debit_amount = valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor` (billed valuation), then compares it with `voucher_wise_stock_value` — the `stock_value_difference` of the invoice's **own SLEs** (fetched at lines 143–152; for a Standard Cost item that's standard rate × qty). Any difference is posted as a "Stock Adjustment" debit to `get_stock_variance_account(item)` (523–533): **the Purchase Price Variance account for Standard Cost items**, else `default_expense_account`. `warehouse_debit_amount` is then reset to the SLE stock value. 2. The main entry (250–269) debits `item.expense_account` — the **inventory account** — with that (standard-cost) amount, against the supplier. The invoice also creates its own Stock Ledger Entries. ## The difference in one line | | Update Stock OFF + PR | Update Stock ON | |---|---|---| | Expense-side debit | **Stock Received But Not Billed** (liability clearing) at billed amount | **Warehouse inventory account** at standard cost | | PPV | None — already booked by the PR (`get_divisional_loss_account` → PPV) | Debit to **PPV account** for billed − standard (`make_stock_adjustment_entry` → `get_stock_variance_account`) | | Stock ledger | None (receipt happened on the PR) | Created by the invoice | Both flows net against the same supplier credit on `credit_to`; the difference is purely *which account absorbs the item's expense side* — the SRBNB clearing account when the PR already did the stock/PPV accounting, versus inventory + PPV when the invoice does the receipt itself.

final answer
## The pattern: a unique secondary sort key appended after the date Whenever ERPNext picks one "latest" row with `ORDER BY <date> DESC LIMIT 1`, the sort is extended with a **unique tiebreaker column** — almost always `creation` (row-creation timestamp) and/or `name` (the document primary key) — so the ORDER BY becomes a **total order**. Ties on the business date are then resolved by a column that cannot tie, and both engines must agree on the winner. A canonical example — `Bin.get_actual_qty` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/bin/bin.py` (lines 303–314): ```python .orderby(sle.posting_datetime, order=Order.desc) .orderby(sle.creation, order=Order.desc) # unique tiebreaker .limit(1) ``` Three variants of the same idea appear in the codebase: 1. **ORDER BY chain + LIMIT 1** — date key first, `creation`/`name` appended (most common). 2. **Total-order predicate** — instead of sorting, the *condition* itself is made unambiguous, e.g. `(mntc_date > X) | ((mntc_date == X) & (mntc_time > X))` in `MaintenanceVisit.check_if_last_visit` (`erpnext/maintenance/doctype/maintenance_visit/maintenance_visit.py`, lines 207–210). 3. **Staged Max() picks in joins** — `SerialNoBundle.get_serial_no_wise_incoming_rate` in `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py` (lines 673–750): an inner query takes `Max(posting_datetime)` per serial no, a second query takes `Max(creation)` among the rows tying on that datetime, and only then joins back for the rate — a two-level tiebreak built from aggregates. ## Why it matters: cross-engine silent divergence ERPNext targets **MariaDB and PostgreSQL from one codebase**, and this exact hazard is codified in the review guide `.github/POSTGRES_COMPATIBILITY.md` (§2, lines 102–104): > **`ORDER BY … LIMIT 1` with no unique tiebreaker** — when rows tie on the ordered column the two engines may pick different rows. Add a `creation`/`name` tiebreaker **only if it does not change MariaDB's current pick** (see §4). Key points: - SQL leaves tie resolution among equal-key rows **undefined**; MariaDB and PostgreSQL (and even different query plans on the same engine) may return different rows. This is a *"silent divergence"* — the guide's failure mode #2: both engines succeed, one-engine CI stays green, but a PostgreSQL site computes a different price, valuation rate, or address. - The companion NULL-ordering rule (§2, lines 100–101) applies to the same shape: MariaDB sorts `NULL` first, Postgres last, so nullable date columns get `Coalesce`/`isnull()` handling before the LIMIT 1 (e.g. `valid_from.isnull()` in `get_item_price`). - §4 (lines 194–196) gives the counter-rule: if the engines already agree, or adding a tiebreaker would *change* MariaDB's current pick, leave it alone — determinism must never alter MariaDB's output, only make an arbitrary pick reproducible. - The mechanical checker `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` lists "ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 tiebreakers" among the patterns it watches; the guide is loaded as Greptile review context via `.greptile/config.json`. - A Postgres-specific wrinkle: when the query is `DISTINCT`, the tiebreaker column must also appear in the SELECT list — handled explicitly in `get_stock_ledgers_for_serial_nos` (`erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`, lines 3425–3429: *"creation is the ORDER BY tiebreaker; postgres requires ORDER BY columns to be in the select list… It is unique per SLE so it doesn't change the distinct row set"*). ## Where it's applied (concrete functions and files) | Function | File | Tiebreaker after the date key | |---|---|---| | `Bin.get_actual_qty` | `erpnext/stock/doctype/bin/bin.py:303` | `posting_datetime desc` → `creation desc` | | `get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos` (staticmethod) | `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1627–1661` | `posting_date desc` → `creation desc` → `name desc` | | `get_valuation_rate` fallback ("last SLE for item+warehouse") | `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:2150–2166` (similar picks at ~2336, ~2438) | `posting_datetime desc` → `creation desc` | | `SerialNoBundle.get_serial_no_wise_incoming_rate` | `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py:673–750` | `Max(posting_datetime)` → `Max(creation)` staged pick | | `get_stock_ledgers_for_serial_nos` | `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py:3408–3434` | `posting_datetime asc` → `creation asc` (+ select-list workaround) | | `get_item_price` | `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1216–1269` | `valid_from desc`, batch/uom/party, then `.orderby(ip.name, desc)` — *"Final unique tiebreaker: rows tied on every sort key above … MariaDB and Postgres can differ. I have the full picture now. Here is the complete answer. ## The pattern: extend the date sort into a *total order* with a unique tiebreaker Every "pick the latest row" query in ERPNext that sorts on a **non-unique** column (`posting_date`, `transaction_date`, `qty`, `valid_from`, `is_primary_contact`, …) appends one or two **unique columns — `creation` and/or `name` (the docname primary key)** — as trailing sort keys. Since no two rows can tie on `name`/`creation`, the composite sort key is unique per row, so `LIMIT 1` returns the same row everywhere, regardless of how the engine orders ties. It appears in two styles: - **Query-builder (`frappe.qb`) — chained `.orderby()` calls**, e.g. `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1653-1656`: ```python .orderby(sle_entry.posting_date, order=frappe.qb.desc) .orderby(sle_entry.creation, order=frappe.qb.desc) .orderby(sle_entry.name, order=frappe.qb.desc) .limit(1) ``` - **Frappe dict API — composite `order_by` string with `limit=1`**, e.g. `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:322`: `order_by="posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc"`. ## Why it matters across engines The rationale is codified in **`.github/POSTGRES_COMPATIBILITY.md`** (ERPNext runs on both MariaDB and PostgreSQL): - **§2, lines 102–104**: *"**`ORDER BY … LIMIT 1` with no unique tiebreaker** — when rows tie on the ordered column the two engines may pick different rows. Add a `creation`/`name` tiebreaker **only if it does not change MariaDB's current pick**"* — SQL leaves the order of tied rows undefined; which row `LIMIT 1` returns depends on storage layout, index choice and the planner, so MariaDB and PostgreSQL can legitimately disagree on identical data. That's a *silent divergence*: both engines succeed, but return different values (§ intro, lines 17–23) — e.g. a different `incoming_rate` for a serial no → different stock valuation, passing CI on one engine and failing on the other. - **The guardrail (§4, lines 194–196)**: if the engines already agree, or adding a tiebreaker would *change* MariaDB's current pick, leave it alone — the fix must only convert an *arbitrary* result into a *deterministic* one without altering existing MariaDB behavior. - **Related engine quirks handled alongside**: NULL ordering (MariaDB sorts NULL first, Postgres last — lines 100–101, hence the `Coalesce(PR.transaction_date, PR.creation)` guard), and Postgres requiring ORDER BY columns of a `DISTINCT` query to appear in the select list (comment at `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py:3426-3429`, where `creation` is added to the SELECT to serve as tiebreaker). The stakes are pinned by a regression test, **`test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic`** (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py:52-98`): *"posting_date alone is non-total, so two same-date SLEs with different incoming_rate could be resolved differently on MariaDB vs Postgres. creation/name tie-breaks make the latest SLE win identically on both engines."* ## Where it is applied — concrete functions and files | Function | File / lines | Sort keys | |---|---|---| | `get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos(sle, serial_nos)` | `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1627-1661` | `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc` → `LIMIT 1` (latest inward SLE for a serial moved to another company) | | `get_balance_qty_from_sle(item_code, warehouse)` | `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:77-84` | `posting_datetime desc, creation desc` | | Stock-reconciliation latest-SLE fetch (in `update_entries_after` setup) | `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:317-325` | `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc` — comment: *"total order so the latest SLE is picked identically on both engines (was posting_date only)"* | | `AssetMovement.get_latest_location_and_custodian(asset)` | `erpnext/assets/doctype/asset_movement/asset_movement.py:128-151` | `transaction_date desc, name desc` → `LIMIT 1` | | `get_payer_address_html(company)` and `get_street_address_html(party_type, party)` | `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py:126-178` | Postal/Billing `Case()` preference, then `.orderby(address.name)` / `.orderby(link.parent)` — *"deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines"*; tested in `test_irs_1099.py` | | `update_packed_item_with_pick_list_info(...)` | `erpnext/stock/doctype/packed_item/packed_item.py:318-338` | `order_by="qty desc, name asc"` — *"name tiebreaker: split pick-list rows can tie on qty"* | | Payment-Request allocation query (called from `PaymentEntry` allocation) | `erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py:2791-2802` | `Coalesce(transaction_date, creation) asc, creation asc, name asc` — *"unique tiebreaker so PRs sharing a transaction_date allocate in the same order on both engines"* | | `get_sle_for_serial_nos(...)` | `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py:3419-3434` | `posting_datetime asc, creation asc` (creation also added to SELECT for Postgres DISTINCT) | | `MaintenanceVisit.update_customer_issue(flag)` | `erpnext/maintenance/doctype/maintenance_visit/maintenance_visit.py:146-162` | `.orderby(mv.name, desc).limit(1)` (name alone is the total order); time-tiebreak branch covered in `test_maintenance_visit.py:69` | | `get_item_price(...)` | `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1265-1267` | final `.orderby(ip.name, desc)` — *"rows tied on every sort key above … MariaDB and Postgres can differ. Pin the pick."* | | POS contact pick | `erpnext/selling/page/point_of_sale/point_of_sale.py:459-467` | `is_primary_contact desc` + tiebreaker for the common no-primary case | | Inactive-customers report | `erpnext/selling/report/inactive_customers/inactive_customers.py:88-89` | `date_col desc, name desc` | | Stock closing | `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_closing_entry/stock_closing_entry.py:345` | `to_date desc, creation desc` | By contrast, queries already sorting on a unique column need no extra key — e.g. `get_last_interaction` in `erpnext/crm/doctype/utils.py` orders Communication by `creation` alone, and its test (`erpnext/crm/doctype/test_utils.py:11-14`) notes explicitly: *"`creation` is unique, so the LIMIT-1 pick is deterministic and identical on MariaDB and Postgres."* **In short:** the guarantee is a codebase-wide convention — never `ORDER BY <non-unique column> LIMIT 1`; always close the sort with `creation`/`name` (optionally behind `Coalesce` for NULLs) so the ordering is a total order, applied across stock valuation, asset tracking, payment allocation, address/report picks and POS, with the policy and its "don't change MariaDB's pick" caveat documented in `.github/POSTGRES_COMPATIBILITY.md` and enforced by engine-portability tests.

final answer
## The pattern: make the sort key a *total order* with unique tie-breakers Every "latest row" pick in this codebase follows the same recipe: order on the business date **first**, then append guaranteed-unique columns — `creation` (Frappe's timestamp column, unique per document) and usually `name` (the primary key) as the final tie-breaker — before `LIMIT 1`: ```sql ORDER BY <business date> DESC, creation DESC, name DESC LIMIT 1 ``` The goal, stated verbatim in the code comments, is a **total order** so the same row wins "identically on both engines" (MariaDB and Postgres). Two representative rationales from the source: - `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:321` — *"total order so the latest SLE is picked identically on both engines (was posting_date only)"* - `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py:52-56` (`test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic`) — *"posting_date alone is non-total, so two same-date SLEs with different incoming_rate could be resolved differently on MariaDB vs Postgres. creation/name tie-breaks make the latest SLE win identically on both engines."* **Why it matters across engines:** the SQL standard leaves row order among ties undefined, and MariaDB and Postgres routinely disagree (different plans, index choices, GROUP BY/DISTINCT behavior) about which tied row comes "first." A bare `ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 1` therefore picks an *arbitrary* row — different exchange rate, stock valuation, or allocated Payment Request depending on the backend. Two engine-specific wrinkles show up too: - Postgres requires ORDER BY columns to appear in the SELECT list of a DISTINCT query, so in `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py:3426-3429` `creation` is explicitly selected ("creation is the ORDER BY tiebreaker… It is unique per SLE") even though it's redundant for the result set. - The inverse case is guarded in `erpnext/selling/page/point_of_sale/point_of_sale.py:331` — a raw query with no ORDER BY suppresses the injected default ordering (`creation desc on MariaDB`) so behavior stays consistent. - When the sort key is already unique (e.g. `creation` alone in `erpnext/crm/doctype/utils.py:29,39,53`, `get_last_interaction`/`get_last_issue_from_customer`), the LIMIT-1 pick is deterministic by construction — the test docstring at `erpnext/crm/doctype/test_utils.py:12-14` spells this out. ## Where it's applied (concrete functions) **Stock valuation / ledger (the highest-stakes uses):** - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` — `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1929`; raw SQL `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update` (line 1959). This anchors sequential SLE valuation under a row lock; a wrong winner here corrupts `qty_after_transaction`/valuation. - `get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos()` — `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1627`; pypika chain `.orderby(posting_date desc).orderby(creation desc).orderby(name desc).limit(1)` (lines 1653–1656). Covered by the tie-break test above, which plants two same-date SLEs (`MAT-SLE-TIE-A`/`-B`) and asserts rate 200 wins on both engines. - `get_balance_qty_from_sle()` — `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:77`, `order_by="posting_datetime desc, creation desc"` (line 82). - `set_stock_balance_as_per_serial_no()` — `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:291`, `order_by="posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc"` (line 322). - `ItemStandardCost.get_last_standard_cost()` (line 255) and `get_item_standard_rate()` (line 291) — `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py`, both `order_by="effective_date desc, creation desc", limit=1` (lines 265, 306). - `StockClosingBalance.get_last_stock_closing_entry()` — `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_closing_entry/stock_closing_entry.py:340`, `order_by="to_date desc, creation desc"` (line 345), so chained closing runs pick the same predecessor. - `get_item_price()` — `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1216`; final `.orderby(ip.name, desc)` (lines 1265–1267): *"rows tied on every sort key above (same valid_from/batch/uom/party) would otherwise be picked arbitrarily — MariaDB and Postgres can differ. Pin the pick."* **Accounts:** - `get_exchange_rate()` — `erpnext/setup/utils.py:62`, `order_by="date desc, name desc", limit=1` (line 101) on Currency Exchange; two rates posted the same day must resolve to one rate everywhere. - `get_open_payment_requests_for_references()` — `erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py:2770`; `.orderby(Coalesce(transaction_date, creation)).orderby(creation).orderby(name)` with the comment *"unique tiebreaker so PRs sharing a transaction_date allocate in the same order on both engines"* (lines 2798–2801) — this drives FIFO allocation order. - `unreconcile_payment.py:135,162,197` — explicit `order_by` added because *"postgres GROUP BY does not imply ordering"*. **Reports/UI picks:** - `get_payer_address_html()` and `get_street_address_html()` — `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py:126,147`; address-type priority CASE ordering followed by `.orderby(address.name)` / `.orderby(link.parent)` — *"deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines"* (lines 134, 158), with coverage in `test_irs_1099.py:15-16`. - POS primary-contact pick — `erpnext/selling/page/point_of_sale/point_of_sale.py:466-469`: `is_primary_contact desc` then `DynamicLink.parent asc` (*"contacts tie on is_primary_contact (the common no-primary case) -> pick the same one on MariaDB and Postgres"*). - `customer_acquisition_and_loyalty.py:169` — *"name tie-break makes the first-seen-per-customer classification deterministic across engines"*; `packed_item.py:329` — same idea for batch/serial assignment; `sales_order_analysis.py:48` — same-day fixes for `delay_days`. **Regression tests pinning the behavior:** `test_stock_ledger_entry.py::test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic` (line 52) and `::test_tie_breaking` (line 1132, asserting `posting_datetime` + `creation` sequencing in reposting), `test_irs_1099.py`, `crm/doctype/test_utils.py::test_get_last_interaction_for_contact`, plus multi-engine assertions in `test_maintenance_visit.py:69` and `test_production_plan.py:3174`. In short: the codebase treats any non-unique ORDER BY + `LIMIT 1` as a latent cross-backend bug, and the house style is to close it by appending `creation` (and `name` where `creation` granularity isn't trusted) to form a total order — turning "the latest row" into a well-defined result on both MariaDB and Postgres.

I have a complete picture now. Here's the synthesis. ## The pattern: a total-order tiebreaker on every `ORDER BY date ... LIMIT 1` pick Whenever ERPNext picks a single "latest" row with `ORDER BY <date> DESC ... LIMIT 1`, the sort keys are extended with columns that make the ordering **total** (no two rows can tie across all keys), so the `LIMIT 1` row is a function of the data, not of the query planner: 1. **`creation DESC`** — Frappe's row-creation timestamp, the primary tiebreaker (unique per row in practice); 2. **`name DESC/ASC`** — the primary key, as the final always-unique key when `creation` alone could still tie (two rows inserted in the same timestamp window). Typical forms found in the code: - Raw SQL: `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1` (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1959`) - query-builder chains: `.orderby(posting_date, posting_time, name, order=Order.desc)` then `.limit(1)` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item/item.py:1392-1400`) ## Why it matters across engines The SQL standard leaves ordering among tied rows undefined, so `ORDER BY x LIMIT 1` with a non-total sort key delegates the winner to the engine's chosen index/scan plan — MariaDB (InnoDB) and Postgres pick different plans and can return **different rows for the same data** when rows share the top date. In ERPNext that divergence leaks into business output (valuation rates, purchase rates, addresses), and it's invisible to static analysis. This repo states this explicitly in the pre-commit guard `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` (docstring, lines 8–11): *"It deliberately does NOT try to catch the semantic divergences (… ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 tiebreakers …) — those genuinely need the test suite or a human/Greptile reviewer."* Postgres also adds a mechanical constraint: when a query is `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` columns must appear in the `SELECT` list — handled in `get_stock_ledgers_for_serial_nos` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py:3426-3429`), which selects `creation` and notes it *"is unique per SLE so it doesn't change the distinct row set."* ## Where it's applied — concrete functions | Function | File | Tiebreaker keys | |---|---|---| | `get_sle_before_datetime()` (backs `get_previous_sle`, the stock-valuation "previous entry" pick, `FOR UPDATE`) | `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1959` | `posting_datetime desc, creation desc` | | `StockLedgerEntry.get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos()` (rate for a serial transferred to another company) | `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1653-1657` | `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc` | | `get_purchase_voucher_details()` (last-purchase rate pick, `LIMIT 1`) | `erpnext/stock/doctype/item/item.py:1392-1400` | `posting_date, posting_time, name desc` (or `transaction_date, name desc`) | | `get_item_price()` (item-price pick, `LIMIT 1`) | `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py:1216`, tiebreaker at :1265-1267 | full key chain ends with `orderby(ip.name, desc)` — commented *"Final unique tiebreaker: rows tied on every sort key above … MariaDB and Postgres can differ. Pin the pick."* | | `get_payer_address_html()` / `get_street_address_html()` (1099 form address pick) | `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py:134,158` | `CASE address_type=Postal/Billing` preference keys + `orderby(address.name)` / `orderby(link.parent)` — *"deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines"* | | `get_open_payment_requests_for_references()` | `erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py:2798-2801` | `Coalesce(transaction_date, creation)` asc, then `creation`, then `name` — *"unique tiebreaker so PRs sharing a transaction_date allocate in the same order on both engines"* | | `get_last_interaction()` (earliest Received communication, `LIMIT 1`) | `erpnext/crm/doctype/utils.py:29-30` | orders by `creation` alone (unique, so total); pinned by its test | | Related report-ordering sites in the same family: `erpnext/accounts/report/utils.py:271,304` (`orderby(je.posting_date, je.name, desc)`), `erpnext/stock/report/stock_ageing/stock_ageing.py:1026`, `erpnext/stock/doctype/delivery_note/services/billing_status.py:93` | | date + `creation`/`name` | ## How it's enforced/tested - **Regression test**: `test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py:52-98`) plants two same-date SLEs for one serial (`MAT-SLE-TIE-A` rate 100, `MAT-SLE-TIE-B` rate 200) and asserts the `creation/name desc` winner (200.0) — its docstring states the rationale verbatim: *"posting_date alone is non-total, so two same-date SLEs with different incoming_rate could be resolved differently on MariaDB vs Postgres."* Also `test_tie_breaking` at :1132. - **Other pinned tests**: `TestCrmDoctypeUtils` (`erpnext/crm/doctype/test_utils.py:11`) and `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/test_irs_1099.py:15` (address preference + `link.parent` tie-break). - **Static guard**: `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` catches the mechanical MySQL-only breaks pre-commit, and explicitly classifies LIMIT-1 tie-breaking as a semantic divergence requiring a Postgres test-suite run — which is why each site carries an inline comment plus a test rather than relying on the hook. In short: the codebase's contract is **every `LIMIT 1` pick must have a total sort order ending in a unique key (`creation`, then `name`)**, because tied dates resolve arbitrarily and differently on MariaDB vs Postgres — a divergence that would otherwise surface as engine-dependent valuations and Postgres-only CI failures.

## Summary On PostgreSQL, this codebase protects reposting/valuation with a layered scheme: **(1) three Postgres-only advisory locks that stand in for MariaDB's gap locks**, **(2) explicit `FOR UPDATE` row locks restructured to be Postgres-legal**, **(3) RQ job-level deduplication/serialization**, and **(4) typed error recovery that re-queues deadlocked jobs**. The key files are `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`, `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`, `erpnext/accounts/utils.py`, and `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py`. ## 1. Postgres-only advisory locks (the core mechanism) Postgres has no gap locks, and `FOR UPDATE` is invalid alongside `GROUP BY`/`DISTINCT` — so MariaDB's implicit serialization doesn't exist there. Three explicit locks compensate: **a) `repost_gate(item_code, warehouse)` — `stock_ledger.py:276`** - A **session-level** `frappe.db.advisory_lock(("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)` taken in `repost_future_sle()` (`stock_ledger.py:335`) around each `update_entries_after(...)` call. It serializes concurrent *background* repost jobs for the same (item, warehouse) **before** they touch the inner row locks, so they "take turns instead of racing into a lock-order deadlock." - `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 300` (`stock_ledger.py:273`) is deliberately below the 1800 s RQ job timeout: a contended worker times out with a recoverable `QueryTimeoutError`, re-queues, and frees the slot. - Scope is intentional: only repost-vs-repost. The synchronous submit path (`repost_current_voucher`, `stock_ledger.py:172`) is *not* gated (blocking a submit behind a background repost would be worse) and keeps relying on the deadlock retry. - Guarded by `hasattr(frappe.db, "advisory_lock")` for graceful opt-in; MariaDB gets `nullcontext()`. **b) `sle_processing_gate(item_code, warehouse)` — `stock_ledger.py:292`** - A **transaction-scoped** `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse))` (released at commit/rollback, re-entrant). Called from: - `update_entries_after.__init__` (`stock_ledger.py:613`) — every repost/valuation run; - `make_sl_entries` (`stock_ledger.py:118-120`) — every stock submission, with the (item, warehouse) pairs **sorted** so two vouchers touching overlapping pairs can't acquire the gates in opposite order (deadlock avoidance). - This prevents *double computation*: on Postgres, locking reads never see rows another transaction is inserting, so without the gate two concurrent writers would both compute from the same stale "previous SLE" and the loser's `Bin` write would be silently lost (`update_bin`, `stock_ledger.py:1891`). **c) Batch average rate — `BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate()` — `serial_batch_bundle.py:818`** - For outward batch entries, before `get_batch_stock_before_date()` runs its `GROUP BY batch_no` history read over `tabSerial and Batch Entry`, it takes a txn-scoped `transaction_advisory_lock(("batch-valuation", item_code, warehouse))` (`serial_batch_bundle.py:828-831`). The grouped query carries `for_update()` only on MariaDB (`serial_batch_bundle.py:894-895`); on Postgres the advisory lock serializes concurrent valuations so the summed `stock_value_difference / qty` (the batch's average incoming rate) can't be computed concurrently from a stale baseline. ## 2. Row locks, restructured to be Postgres-legal - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` (`stock_ledger.py:1929`) — raw SQL `... limit 1 for update` locking the previous SLE that seeds the valuation. - `get_sle_against_current_voucher` (`stock_ledger.py:1906`) and `get_stock_ledger_entries(..., for_update=True)` (`stock_ledger.py:1994`) — locked reads of current/future SLEs during reposting. - `get_future_stock_vouchers` (`erpnext/accounts/utils.py:1772`) — since Postgres rejects `FOR UPDATE` with `GROUP BY`, it first runs a separate `select ConstantColumn(1) ... .for_update()` pass over the matching SLE rows (holding them to transaction end; a deep repost can match millions of rows, so only locks are selected), then does the `GROUP BY voucher_type, voucher_no` query unlocked. MariaDB keeps `for_update()` on the grouped query. This keeps rows stable for the whole repost so a concurrent transaction can't modify them mid-flight. ## 3. Job-level deduplication — `repost_item_valuation.py` - `enqueue_reposting_entry` (`:828`) uses deterministic `job_id="repost_item_valuation_entry_{name}"` with `deduplicate=True` — one RQ job per Repost Item Valuation doc. - `run_parallel_reposting` (`:791`, hook-scheduled, self-rescheduling via `enqueue_parallel_reposting`) skips entries with active jobs (`get_entries_with_active_jobs` `:850`, `get_items_with_active_reposting` `:860`) and caps concurrency at `no_of_parallel_reposting` distinct items, never enqueueing two jobs for the same item. - `deduplicate_similar_repost` (`:322`) marks other `Queued` "Item and Warehouse" reposts for the same item+warehouse with a *later* posting datetime as `Skipped`; `skip_reposts_covered_by_dependents` (`:354`) plus the coverage data in `reposting_data_file`/`item_wh_first_reposted` avoid recomputation already done by a dependent repost. - Within one job, `repost_future_sle` (`stock_ledger.py:304`) processes items one gate at a time and checkpoints progress (`update_args_in_repost_item_valuation`), so interrupted reposts resume rather than recompute. ## 4. Recovery instead of failure `repost()` (`repost_item_valuation.py:530`) classifies exceptions against `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)` (`:36`) — deadlocks and lock/query timeouts re-queue the doc as `In Progress` instead of `Failed` (the comment notes the old traceback string-match missed Postgres's "deadlock detected" message and permanently failed such jobs). **Net effect on Postgres:** concurrent background reposts of the same (item, warehouse) are serialized by the `stock_repost` advisory lock (turn-taking, no lock-order deadlock); the `stock-sle` and `batch-valuation` txn-scoped locks guarantee only one writer computes valuation/average rate from a given ledger baseline (no lost Bin/batch-avg updates); row locks keep the SLE history stable for the transaction; and anything that still deadlocks or times out is retried rather than failing.

Here's how the stock reposting/valuation subsystem keeps concurrent Postgres background jobs from deadlocking or double-computing batch average rates. ## Overview When parallel reposting is enabled (`Stock Reposting Settings.enable_parallel_reposting`), multiple RQ workers on the `long` queue each run a `Repost Item Valuation` doc through `repost()` → `repost_sl_entries()` → `repost_future_sle()` → `update_entries_after` per (item, warehouse). On PostgreSQL the locking reads that MariaDB relies on behave differently (no gap locks; `FOR UPDATE` is invalid with `GROUP BY`), so ERPNext layers **three Postgres-only advisory locks, job-level deduplication, and deadlock-aware error classification** on top of the usual `FOR UPDATE` row locks. ## 1. Job-level dedup — never two jobs on the same entry/item `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py`: - `enqueue_reposting_entry()` (line 828) enqueues each entry with `job_id=f"repost_item_valuation_entry_{name}"` and `deduplicate=True` — the same repost entry can't be queued twice. - `run_parallel_reposting()` (line 791) consults `get_entries_with_active_jobs()` (line 850), which scans RQ's queued + started job registries for the `REPOSTING_JOB_ID_PREFIX` prefix, and skips entries already running. It *also* skips any entry whose `item_code` appears in `get_items_with_active_reposting()` (line 860) — so **only one active repost job per item code** across all queued entries, capped at `no_of_parallel_reposting`. Finished jobs re-trigger the picker (`execute_reposting_entry` → `finally: enqueue_parallel_reposting()`), with a 15-min hooks.py cron as a recovery net. - `_execute_reposting_entry()` (line 896) only processes docs whose status is `Queued`/`In Progress`; `repost()` (line 530) flips status to `In Progress` and **commits before** starting the heavy work. ## 2. `repost_gate` — the deadlock preventer `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`, lines 269–289: - `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 300` (deliberately well under the 1800s job timeout, so a contended worker re-queues via a recoverable `QueryTimeoutError` instead of pinning its slot). - `repost_future_sle()` (line 335) wraps every per-(item, warehouse) `update_entries_after(...)` call in `with repost_gate(item_code, warehouse)`. - Postgres only: `if frappe.db.db_type == "postgres" and hasattr(frappe.db, "advisory_lock")` — it takes a **session-level advisory lock keyed `("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse)`** (tuple key so a colon in item/warehouse names can't collide two pairs onto one lock); otherwise it returns `nullcontext()`. - Its job (per the docstring): serialize **repost-vs-repost** for the same (item, warehouse) *before* the inner `... for update` row-lock reads are taken, so concurrent reposts take turns instead of acquiring the SLE row locks in conflicting orders and tracing into a lock-order deadlock. Row locks still enforce correctness; the gate only cuts the deadlock/retry churn. The synchronous submit path (`repost_current_voucher`) is deliberately **not** gated — blocking a user submit behind a background repost would be worse — and MariaDB keeps the plain deadlock-retry path (InnoDB gap locks already serialize there). ## 3. `sle_processing_gate` — serialize all stock writes per (item, warehouse) `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`, lines 292–301: - A **transaction-scoped, re-entrant** advisory lock keyed `("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse)` (`frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock`, released at commit/rollback). - Called from two places: `update_entries_after.__init__` (line 613) and — importantly — `make_sl_entries` (lines 118–120), which takes the gates for the **sorted** set of `(item_code, warehouse)` pairs before writing, so two vouchers touching the same pairs can never take the gates in opposite order (the classic deadlock-avoidance trick). - Rationale: MariaDB's previous-SLE locking reads take gap locks that block *and reveal* concurrent inserts; Postgres locking reads never see rows another transaction is inserting, so without this gate two concurrent writers compute from the same stale previous SLE and the loser's `Bin` update is silently lost. ## 4. Row-lock backstop reads (correctness) Inside the gate, `update_entries_after` still row-locks what it recomputes: `initialize_previous_data` → `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` ends with raw SQL `limit 1 for update` (line 1961), `get_sle_against_current_voucher()` uses `.for_update()` (line 1920), and the future entries to be reposted are read with `for_update=True` via `get_sle_after_datetime()` → `get_stock_ledger_entries()` (lines 1831, 2075). Only `get_sle_before_datetime()` reads without `for update` (line 1825) — the previous SLE is protected by the advisory gates instead. ## 5. The batch average-rate lock — no double-computing `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`, `BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate()` (lines 818–845): - For **outward** transactions (`actual_qty <= 0`), before reading the batch history it takes `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("batch-valuation", self.sle.item_code, self.sle.warehouse))` — again **Postgres only** (line 828–831). This is the lock that prevents two jobs (or a job and a synchronous valuation) from computing the same batch's moving average concurrently: the second contender blocks, and when it proceeds it reads history that already includes the first one's committed bundle values, rather than both computing from the same snapshot. - Why an advisory lock here at all: in `get_batch_stock_before_date()` (lines 881–897) the grouped history query gets `.for_update()` **only on non-Postgres** (`if frappe.db.db_type != "postgres": query = query.for_update()`), because on Postgres `FOR UPDATE` is invalid with `GROUP BY`, there are no gap locks, and row-locking the whole history would write a lock marker on every tuple. MariaDB gets its serialization from those grouped `FOR UPDATE` + gap locks instead. - This path is reached both from reposting (`update_entries_after.update_batched_values` line 1759, `update_serial_batch_no_valuation` line 1265) and synchronous valuation (`get_valuation_rate` in stock_ledger.py line 2096, `get_incoming_rate` in stock/utils.py line 244). ## 6. Last-resort: deadlocks/timeouts re-queue instead of failing `repost_item_valuation.py` line 36: `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)`. In `repost()`'s exception handler (lines 563–605), the doc is rolled back, the error logged, and status set to **`In Progress`** (retryable) if the exception is one of these — with classification by exception *type*, because the old traceback string-match only knew MariaDB's "Deadlock found" and missed Postgres's "deadlock detected" (see the test at `test_repost_item_valuation.py` lines 370–397). Only non-recoverable errors mark the entry `Failed` and email the Stock Manager. So even if a deadlock slips past the gates, the repost is retried rather than lost. **In short:** deduplication at enqueue time (job ID + per-item exclusion) reduces concurrency; the session-level `repost_gate` per (item, warehouse) makes background reposts take turns before touching row locks (deadlock prevention); the txn-scoped `sle_processing_gate` and `("batch-valuation", ...)` lock serialize stock writes and batch average-rate computation on Postgres where gap locks and `FOR UPDATE ... GROUP BY` don't exist; row locks remain the correctness backstop; and `RecoverableErrors` handling turns any residual deadlock/timeout into a re-queue rather than a failure.

On PostgreSQL, concurrency control is done with **advisory locks keyed on (item_code, warehouse)**, plus a recoverable-error retry ladder and queue-level deduplication. The Postgres-specific code is deliberately gated behind `frappe.db.db_type == "postgres"` checks with `hasattr` fallbacks, because MariaDB solves the same problems with gap locks + deadlock-retry instead. ## 1. The three Postgres advisory-lock gates (all in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`) **a) `repost_gate(item_code, warehouse)` (line 276) — prevents repost-vs-repost deadlocks.** A **session-level** advisory lock keyed `("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse)` with a `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 300`s wait. `repost_future_sle()` takes it (line 335) around each `update_entries_after(...)` call: ```python with repost_gate(item_code, warehouse): obj = update_entries_after({...}) ``` The docstring states the intent: concurrent background reposts of the same (item, warehouse) *"take turns instead of racing into a lock-order deadlock"*. The gate is acquired **before** the inner `... for update` row locks, so two repost jobs never interleave their row-lock acquisition order on the same item-warehouse history. Row locks still enforce correctness; the gate only *"cuts the deadlock/retry churn"*. If the 300s wait expires, the job gets a `QueryTimeoutError`, which (see layer 3) is treated as recoverable — the contended worker re-queues and frees the slot rather than pinning it. The timeout is deliberately kept under the 1800s job timeout. **b) `sle_processing_gate(item_code, warehouse)` (line 292) — prevents lost/duplicated state across *all* writers.** A **transaction-scoped** advisory lock `("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse)` (released at commit/rollback, re-entrant). This exists because of a Postgres-specific behavior: *"MariaDB gets [serialization] from the gap locks its previous-SLE locking reads take (which also block, then reveal, concurrent inserts); postgres locking reads never see rows another transaction is inserting, so without this gate two concurrent writers compute from the same stale previous SLE and the loser's Bin write is lost."* It's taken at: - `make_sl_entries()` (line 104–120) — every stock write, with **pairs sorted** before locking so two vouchers touching the same item-warehouse pairs can never take the gates in opposite order (classic deadlock-avoidance via total lock ordering); - `update_entries_after.__init__()` (line 613) — the reposting engine itself gates before reading prior SLE state. **c) The batch-valuation lock — the direct answer to "double-computing the average rate."** In `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`, `BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate()` (line 818) serializes **outward** (consumption) transactions before they read batch history: ```python if frappe.db.db_type == "postgres": frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock( ("batch-valuation", self.sle.item_code, self.sle.warehouse) ) ``` Why: the history read `get_batch_stock_before_date()` (line 847) does a `GROUP BY batch_no` with `SUM(stock_value_difference)`/`SUM(qty)` — **`FOR UPDATE` is invalid with `GROUP BY` on Postgres**, and row-locking the whole history would write a lock marker on every tuple. So on Postgres the advisory lock replaces it (`if frappe.db.db_type != "postgres": query = query.for_update()`, line 894), while on MariaDB the grouped `FOR UPDATE` + gap locks do the serialization. Result: two concurrent valuations of the same (item, warehouse) can't both read the same pre-transaction batch balances and compute overlapping average rates — the second waits for commit/rollback, then reads the first's committed history. The same pattern exists in the deprecated path, `erpnext/stock/deprecated_serial_batch.py:147-160`. ## 2. Correctness is still enforced by row locks The advisory gates are only churn-reducers; the ledger reads still lock rows: `get_stock_ledger_entries(..., for_update=True)` appends literal `"for update"` to the SQL (stock_ledger.py:2072–2075, used for future-SLE reads at line 904), `get_sle_against_current_voucher()` (line 1906–1926) and `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` (line 1929–1970) both end in `for update`. Note the deliberate scoping: `repost_gate` covers **repost-vs-repost only** — the synchronous `repost_current_voucher` submit path is *not* gated, since blocking a user submit behind a background repost would be a worse regression; it keeps relying on the existing deadlock retry. ## 3. Deadlock tolerance at the job layer (`repost_item_valuation.py`) `repost()` classifies exceptions with `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)` (line 36). On failure: ```python # Recoverable errors (deadlock, lock/query timeout, job timeout) re-queue as In Progress. # Classify by type: the old traceback string-match only knew MariaDB's "Deadlock found" and # missed Postgres deadlocks ("deadlock detected"), failing them permanently. status = "In Progress" if isinstance(e, RecoverableErrors) else "Failed" ``` So even if a Postgres deadlock slips through the gates, the RIV is rolled back and re-queued as "In Progress" instead of permanently "Failed". (This exception-type classification is itself the Postgres fix — string-matching `"Deadlock found"` missed Postgres's `"deadlock detected"` message.) ## 4. Queue-level deduplication prevents concurrency from ever arising In `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py`: - **One job per item, deduplicated jobs:** `run_parallel_reposting()` (line 791) skips entries that already have an active rq job (`get_entries_with_active_jobs()` scans job IDs `repost_item_valuation_entry_{name}` in the "long" queue), and `get_items_with_active_reposting()` guarantees at most one in-flight repost per `item_code`, up to `no_of_parallel_reposting` (default 4). `enqueue_reposting_entry()` uses `job_id=...` with `deduplicate=True`. - **Status machine:** `repost()` flips the RIV to "In Progress" and commits *before* doing work, so other pickers skip in-flight entries; on completion it calls `deduplicate_similar_repost()` (line 322), which marks any later-posting **Queued** RIVs for the same item+warehouse as **"Skipped"** (using the portable `CombineDatetime()` comparison instead of MySQL-only `TIMESTAMP()`) — the same valuation never recomputes twice. - **Coverage-based skipping:** `skip_reposts_covered_by_dependents()` / `mark_covered_item_reposts()` / `mark_covered_transaction_reposts()` skip queued reposts fully covered by a just-completed one, tracked per-RIV in the cache under `riv_dependent_coverage::{name}`. ## Verification Tests assert the locks actually appear in `pg_locks`: `test_stock_write_takes_sle_advisory_gate` (`test_stock_ledger_entry.py:37`) and `test_outward_batch_valuation_takes_transaction_advisory_lock` (`test_serial_and_batch_bundle.py:204`) both `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype = 'advisory'` around a stock write/valuation. **In short:** Postgres lacks MariaDB's gap locks, so the subsystem compensates with (1) a session-scoped `("stock_repost", item, warehouse)` advisory gate taken before row locks to serialize concurrent reposts turn-by-turn, (2) a transaction-scoped `("stock-sle", item, warehouse)` gate around every stock write with **sorted lock ordering**, (3) a transaction-scoped `("batch-valuation", item, warehouse)` gate in `calculate_avg_rate` that replaces MariaDB's grouped `FOR UPDATE` so two jobs can't compute the same batch average rate from stale history, and (4) belt-and-braces at the queue level — type-based deadlock classification that re-queues instead of failing, rq job deduplication, and one-active-repost-per-item scheduling.

All the pieces are confirmed. Here's the complete answer. ## How PostgreSQL stock reposting avoids deadlocks / double-computed average rates The subsystem uses a **layered strategy**: job-level dedup → per-(item, warehouse) Postgres advisory locks → row locks as the correctness backstop → deadlock-aware retry/resume. The Postgres-specific parts are all new/opt-in code gated on `frappe.db.db_type == "postgres"`; MariaDB keeps its old gap-lock + deadlock-retry behavior. ### 1. Never start two jobs on the same work (`repost_item_valuation.py`) - `enqueue_reposting_entry()` (line 828) enqueues with `job_id=f"repost_item_valuation_entry_{name}"` and `deduplicate=True` — RQ won't run a duplicate job for the same *Repost Item Valuation* doc (`test_enqueue_reposting_entry_is_deduplicated` asserts this). - `run_parallel_reposting()` (line 791, recovery cron every 15 min + chained after each job) picks entries with status `Queued`/`In Progress` (`get_repost_item_valuation_entries`, line 911), skips docs that already have active jobs (`get_entries_with_active_jobs` inspects the "long" queue's job/started registries), and — key for your question — **skips any entry whose `item_code` already has an active reposting job** (`get_items_with_active_reposting`), so it never schedules two repost workers against the same item concurrently. ### 2. `repost_gate()` — session-level advisory lock per (item, warehouse) (`stock_ledger.py:276`) In `repost_future_sle`'s per-item loop (line 335), each `(item_code, warehouse)` repost is wrapped in: ```python with repost_gate(item_code, warehouse): # frappe.db.advisory_lock(("stock_repost", item, wh), timeout=300) obj = update_entries_after(...) ``` The docstring states it directly: it **serializes concurrent background reposts of the same (item, warehouse)** with a session-level advisory lock taken **before** the inner `... for update` row locks, "so they take turns instead of racing into a lock-order deadlock. Row locks still enforce correctness; this only cuts the deadlock/retry churn." It's repost-vs-repost only (the synchronous `repost_current_voucher` submit path deliberately isn't gated), Postgres-only, with a graceful `hasattr(frappe.db, "advisory_lock")` fallback, and `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 300`s — kept under the 1800s job timeout so a contended worker re-queues instead of pinning the slot. ### 3. `sle_processing_gate()` — txn-scoped lock for every stock write (`stock_ledger.py:292`) A transaction-scoped, re-entrant advisory lock `("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse)` (released at commit/rollback), taken in two places: - `update_entries_after.__init__` (line 613) — the whole repost computation for that (item, warehouse); - `make_sl_entries` (lines 117–120) — before writing any SLEs, for **every** (item, warehouse) pair in the batch, **sorted** ("so two vouchers touching the same pairs can't take the gates in opposite order" — classic lock-ordering deadlock prevention). Rationale (docstring): MariaDB's previous-SLE locking reads take gap locks that also block concurrent inserts; **Postgres locking reads never see rows another transaction is inserting**, so without this gate "two concurrent writers compute from the same stale previous SLE and the loser's Bin write is lost." ### 4. The direct answer to double-computed *batch average rate* — `BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate` (`serial_batch_bundle.py:818`) For an **outward** entry (`actual_qty <= 0`), before reading the batch history and computing moving-average rates: ```python if frappe.db.db_type == "postgres": frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock( ("batch-valuation", self.sle.item_code, self.sle.warehouse) ) ``` On MariaDB, the grouped history queries (`get_batch_stock_before_date`, and the deprecated equivalents in `deprecated_serial_batch.py` — `get_sle_for_batches`, `set_balance_value_from_bundle`, etc.) carry `FOR UPDATE` + gap locks to serialize this; **on Postgres `FOR UPDATE` is invalid with `GROUP BY`** and row-locking the whole history would write a lock marker on every tuple, so those queries drop `.for_update()` when `db_type == "postgres"` (e.g. serial_batch_bundle.py:894, deprecated_serial_batch.py:159, 292) and the txn-scoped advisory lock on `(item, warehouse)` replaces that serialization. This lock is what stops two concurrent background repost jobs from reading the same pre-state and both writing `incoming_rate`/`stock_value_difference` for the same item-warehouse batch valuation. (`test_outward_batch_valuation_takes_transaction_advisory_lock` in `test_serial_and_batch_bundle.py:204` verifies the lock is held; `pick_list.py:558` uses the same pattern with a `("pick-allocate", item_code)` key.) ### 5. Row locks remain the correctness backstop `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` (stock_ledger.py:1961) ends its latest-previous-SLE query with `for update`, and `get_sle_against_current_voucher` (line 1920) uses `.for_update()` — so genuine conflicts still serialize on rows; the advisory gates exist only to prevent AB-BA deadlocks and stale-read races, not to replace row-level correctness. ### 6. Recovery when contention still surfaces — `repost()` (`repost_item_valuation.py:530`) - `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)` (line 36). On such an error the job rolls back and sets the doc's status back to **"In Progress"** (not "Failed") so the recovery cron re-picks it. A comment notes the old traceback string-match only knew MariaDB's "Deadlock found" and **missed Postgres's "deadlock detected"**, failing reposts permanently — this fork classifies by exception type instead (`test_repost_item_valuation.py:368–397` asserts `QueryDeadlockError("deadlock detected") → "In Progress"`). - Lock waits are bounded (300s), so contention degrades into a re-queued, recoverable `QueryTimeoutError` rather than burning the job budget. - Resumability: status "In Progress" is committed **before** reposting starts (line 539–541), and after every (item, warehouse) iteration `update_args_in_repost_item_valuation` (stock_ledger.py:368) persists `current_index` + the reposting-data file and commits — a retried job resumes via `get_current_index(doc)` at the exact item it died on, so work isn't redone. On success, `deduplicate_similar_repost()` / `skip_reposts_covered_by_dependents()` mark redundant queued RIVs "Skipped". - `patches/v13_0/requeue_recoverable_reposts.py` requeues historically "Failed" reposts that actually hit these recoverable errors. **In one sentence:** parallel-repost scheduling dedups jobs per doc and per item, a session-level `("stock_repost", item, warehouse)` advisory lock makes same-pair background reposts take turns (avoiding lock-order deadlocks before the `for update` row locks), transaction-scoped `("stock-sle", ...)` and `("batch-valuation", item, warehouse)` advisory locks serialize SLE writes and the batch average-rate computation (replacing MariaDB's `FOR UPDATE`/gap-lock behavior, which Postgres can't express on `GROUP BY` history queries), and any residual deadlock/timeout is classified as recoverable and re-queued with per-item resume state rather than failing.

## Short answer Concurrency safety is done with **database row-level locking — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` — combined with a status state machine (`Queued` → `Running` → `Completed`) and `enqueue_after_commit=True` job dispatch**, so a (date, report_type) row can only ever be "claimed" by one worker transaction at a time. ## Where it lives All of this is in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/process_period_closing_voucher/process_period_closing_voucher.py`, with the child table rows in `process_period_closing_voucher_detail.py`. ## The full flow 1. **Work is pre-split into rows.** When the PCV is submitted, `Period Closing Voucher.on_submit` (`period_closing_voucher.py:136-140`) creates a `Process Period Closing Voucher` (PPCV) doc. Its `validate()` → `populate_processing_tables()` → `generate_pcv_dates()` appends one child row in `normal_balances` for **every day in the period × each report type** (`"Profit and Loss"` and `"Balance Sheet"`), all with `status: "Queued"`; for the first PCV of the company, `generate_opening_balances_dates()` also fills `z_opening_balances` (rows keyed by `processing_date` + `report_type` + `parentfield`). 2. **Workers claim rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.** `on_submit` → `start_pcv_processing()` → `initialize_parallel_threads(docname)`. That function runs: ```python qb.from_(ppcvd).select(...) .where(ppcvd.parent.eq(docname) & ppcvd.status.eq("Queued")) .orderby(ppcvd.parentfield, ppcvd.idx, ppcvd.processing_date) .limit(threads) # threads = 4 .for_update(skip_locked=True) .run(as_dict=True) ``` `for_update(skip_locked=True)` emits `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. If two scheduler/worker transactions run this simultaneously, the DB gives the row locks to whichever transaction gets there first, and the other transaction **silently skips locked rows** — it can never select, and therefore never enqueue, a `(processing_date, report_type)` row that another worker is already claiming. Each claimer immediately sets its rows to `"Running"` inside that same transaction. 3. **The claim is committed before the job is picked up.** Jobs are enqueued with `enqueue_after_commit=True`, and an explicit `frappe.db.commit()` is issued right after setting `"Running"` (with the comment *"keep transaction on PPCV and PPCVD short / prevents concurrency errors - REPEATABLE READ"*). So by the time a RQ worker executes `process_individual_date`, the row's `Running` status is durably committed — no other claim query can see it as `Queued`. 4. **Defensive re-check inside the job.** `process_individual_date()` starts by re-reading the row status and returns immediately unless it is still `"Running"` — a stale/duplicate job can't reprocess an already-claimed or cancelled row. 5. **Chained dispatch replaces a fixed worker pool.** When a worker finishes, it writes its computed `closing_balance` JSON, marks the row `"Completed"`, commits, and then calls `schedule_next_date(docname)`, which claims the **next single** `Queued` row using the exact same `.for_update(skip_locked=True).limit(1)` pattern and enqueues it. This chain keeps up to ~4 workers busy while guaranteeing one-owner-per-row; when no `Queued` rows remain and `total_no_of_dates == completed`, it enqueues the final `summarize_and_post_ledger_entries` job — deduplicated by the RQ job name `summarize_{docname}` via `is_job_running(job_name)`. 6. **Supporting bits:** `on_doctype_update()` in the detail doctype adds a composite index on `(parent, status, parentfield, idx, processing_date)` so the lock-and-claim query is cheap; `pause_/cancel_/resume_pcv_processing()` only flip row statuses (`Paused`/`Cancelled` → `Queued` on resume), so the same lock-based claim protocol governs restarts too. So the guarantee comes from the database, not from the job queue: the `(parent, status="Queued")` claim query with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` makes row acquisition atomic across worker transactions, the committed `Running` flag makes the claim visible and irreversible to everyone else, and `enqueue_after_commit=True` + the `status == "Running"` re-check close the race window between claiming and job execution.
